Graphon Mean-Field Subsampling for Cooperative Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Emile Anand Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA Correspondence to: emiletimothy@outlook.com    Richard Hoffmann Affiliation: Computing and Mathematical Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA    Sarah Liaw Affiliation: Kempner Institute, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA    Adam Wierman Affiliation: Computing and Mathematical Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA
Abstract

Coordinating large populations of interacting agents is a central challenge in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), where the size of the joint state-action space scales exponentially with the number of agents. Mean-field methods alleviate this burden by aggregating agent interactions, but these approaches assume homogeneous interactions. Recent graphon-based frameworks capture heterogeneity, but are computationally expensive as the number of agents grows. Therefore, we introduce GMFS, a Graphon Mean-Field Subsampling framework for scalable cooperative MARL with heterogeneous agent interactions. By subsampling κ\kappa agents according to interaction strength, we approximate the graphon-weighted mean-field and learn a policy with sample complexity poly⁡(κ)\mathrm{poly}(\kappa) and optimality gap O~​(1/κ)\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{\kappa}). We verify our theory with numerical simulations in robotic coordination, showing that GMFS achieves near-optimal performance.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling complex, large-scale networked systems whose dynamics stem from the interactions between many individual agents. These systems are now ubiquitous, appearing in domains as varied as robotic swarms (Lv et al., 2025; Aina and Ha, 2025; Chiun et al., 2025; Preiss et al., 2017), autonomous driving (Kiran et al., 2021; Kiran et al., 2022; Shalev-Shwartz et al., 2016; DeWeese and Qu, 2024), ride-sharing (Li et al., 2019), real-time bidding (Jin et al., 2018), stochastic games (Jin et al., 2020; Chaudhari et al., 2025), and efficient wireless networks (Cui et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2025). In these settings, the objective is to derive optimal policies that maximize collective reward across the entire system. Drawing on the success of reinforcement learning (RL) in tasks like the game of Go (Silver et al., 2016) and robotic control (Kober et al., 2013), MARL extends these ideas to environments with multiple interacting agents. However, quickly solving such systems exactly becomes infeasible as the number of agents grows, creating a barrier to large-scale deployment.

The primary challenge in scaling MARL lies in the size of the joint state-action space (|𝒮|​|𝒜|)n(|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|)^{n}, which grows exponentially with the population size nn and renders exhaustive sampling over all agents computationally intractable (Blondel and Tsitsiklis, 2000). To mitigate this “curse of dimensionality”, previous works proposed using mean-field theory to approximate agent populations by replacing explicit interactions with population aggregates (Yang et al., 2018; Carmona et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; Cui et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2025). However, these frameworks typically require iterating over the entire population at each time step to compute aggregates. More recently, Anand et al. (2025a) mitigate this cost by sampling a subset of kk agents to achieve polynomial complexity. However, these standard mean-field methods often fail at capturing the heterogeneous behaviors inherent in complex systems like traffic management (Zheng et al., 2025). As noted by Carmona et al. (2021), ignoring agent diversity can lead to systemic failures, including communication delays (Singh et al., 2025; Rahimi and Esfanjani, 2023), inefficient information dissemination (Olfati-Saber et al., 2007), and unstable robotic control (Yi et al., 2016).

To model these non-uniformities, Lovász (2012); Gao and Caines (2017); Caines and Huang (2021) represent network systems via graphons, where a limit function W⁡(x,y)W(x,y) defines interaction strengths between agents on a latent index x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1]. Although Hu et al. (2023) established an approximation error bound of O⁡(1/n)O(1/\sqrt{n}) for such systems, no existing framework unifies the computational efficiency of neighborhood subsampling with the expressiveness of graphon-level heterogeneity. Therefore, we ask:

Can a mean-field MARL algorithm handle heterogeneity through non-uniform agent interactions, while reducing computation to a polylogarithmic dependence on the number of agents?

1.1 Contributions

Our key contributions are outlined below.

  • •

    GMFS Algorithm (§3). We introduce a subsampling framework for cooperative MARL with heterogeneous agents, where graphon mean-field interactions are approximated using κ≪n\kappa\ll n sampled neighbors.

  • •

    Theoretical Guarantees (§4, §5). We bound the optimality gap between the κ\kappa-sampled policy and the optimal graphon mean-field policy. For finite state-action spaces, we show that GMFS reduces the sample complexity from exponential in nn, (|𝒮|n​|𝒜|n|\mathcal{S}|^{n}|\mathcal{A}|^{n}), to polynomial in κ\kappa, (κ|𝒮|​|𝒜|\kappa^{|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|}).

  • •

    Numerical Simulations (§A). We observe monotonic improvements in average discounted return as κ\kappa increases, approaching the exhaustive mean-field limit in a heterogeneous robot-warehouse environment.

A crucial challenge in heterogeneous systems is the position-dependent variance that makes uniform sampling ineffective. We show how to resolve this issue via graphon-weighted subsampling, where neighbors are sampled directly according to normalized graphon weights. By showing that the resulting sampled Bellman operator remains a γ\gamma-contraction, we prove that the algorithm converges to an approximately optimal policy. We further show that the optimality gap concentrates at an O⁡(1/κ)O(1/\sqrt{\kappa}) rate (Theorem C.3), unifying uniform mean-field and exhaustive population methods.

1.2 Related Literature

MARL has a rich history, beginning with early work on Markov games for multi-agent decision-making (Littman, 1994; Sutton et al., 1999), which can be viewed as multi-agent extensions of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Since then, MARL has been studied across a wide range of settings (Zhang et al., 2021). It is closely related to “succinctly described” MDPs (Blondel and Tsitsiklis, 2000), where the joint state-action space is a product of individual agent spaces and agents optimize a collective objective. A promising recent line of work constrains such problems to sparse networked instances to enforce local interactions (Qu et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2020; Mondal et al., 2022).In this formulation, agents correspond to graph vertices and interact only with immediate neighbors. By exploiting correlation decay (Gamarnik et al., 2014), these methods mitigate the curse of dimensionality by searching over policies defined on truncated graphs. Yet, as networks become dense, agent neighborhoods grow, rendering graph-truncation approaches computationally intractable.

Mean-Field RL. To address large agent neighborhoods, mean-field theory replaces a finite set of local agents with an empirical distribution over agent states (Lasry and Lions, 2007; Yang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2023). This simplifies multi-agent interactions into a two-agent formulation, where each agent interacts with a representative “mean agent” that evolves according to the empirical distribution of all other agents (Gu et al., 2025). For a detailed overview of learning methodologies in mean-field games, we refer the reader to Laurière et al. (2022). Pásztor et al. (2023) explore efficient model-based approaches to further improve sample efficiency in these settings. By sampling a subset of the total population, Anand et al. (2025a) build on this mean-field abstraction to achieve a sample complexity that is polynomial in the number of subsampled agents. However, these approaches operate under the assumption that interactions between agents are uniform. Our GMFS algorithm utilizes graphon functions to model heterogeneous interactions in dense graphs, better representing realistic networked systems (Fabian et al., 2023) while maintaining provable performance guarantees.

Graphon Mean-Field MARL. Building on classical mean-field MARL, a growing body of recent work relaxes homogeneity assumptions by modeling dense, heterogeneous interactions in large populations. Caines and Huang (2018) introduced Graphon Mean-Field Games (GMFG), formalizing graphons as limiting objects that encode heterogeneous structures in infinite networks (Borgs et al., 2007). Subsequent work expands GMFG concepts to broader classes of control and learning problems, including dynamical sequential games (Cui and Koeppl, 2022; Fabian et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023), learning algorithms for realistic sparse graphs (Fabian et al., 2025), and graphon estimation from sampled agents (Zhang et al., 2024a; Fabian et al., 2022). Moreover, even when the graphon is unknown, it can be efficiently estimated (Chan and Airoldi, 2014; Airoldi et al., 2013). In the cooperative MARL setting, Hu et al. (2023) adapts the GMFG framework to Graphon Mean-Field Control, where agents optimize a joint QQ-function driven by graphon-weighted aggregates. While these works demonstrate that graphons provide a principled mechanism for capturing heterogeneity, existing methods typically require full population aggregation at each time step. In contrast, GMFS approximates these aggregates using only κ<n\kappa<n sampled neighbors.

Structured RL. Our work is also related to factored and exogenous MDPs. In factored MDPs, a global action typically affects every agent, whereas in our setting, each agent selects its own action (Min et al., 2023). Our approach shares similarities with MDPs involving exogenous inputs (Dietterich et al., 2018; Foster et al., 2022), as our subsampling algorithm treats sampled states as endogenous while allowing for dynamic exogenous dependencies.

Other Related Work. Beyond the areas highlighted above, our work contributes to the literature on Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (Zhou et al., 2023), as we learn a provably near-optimal policy using centralized information while executing decisions based only on local observations. In distributed settings, V-learning (Jin et al., 2020) reduces the exponential dependence on the joint action space to an additive one. In contrast, our approach further reduces the complexity of the joint state space, which has not been previously achieved. Finally, while linear function approximation can be used to reduce QQ-table complexity (Jin et al., 2020), bounding the resulting performance loss is generally intractable without strong assumptions such as Linear Bellman completeness (Golowich and Moitra, 2024) or low Bellman-Eluder dimension (Jin et al., 2021). While our work primarily considers the finite tabular setting, we also provide extensions to the non-tabular case under Linear Bellman completeness.

2 Preliminaries

We formally introduce the problem, state motivating examples for our setting, and provide technical details about the mean-field model and graphon-based techniques used.

Notation. For n,κ∈ℕn,\kappa\in\mathbb{N} with κ≤n\kappa\leq n, let ([n]κ)\binom{[n]}{\kappa} denote the set of all κ\kappa-sized subsets of [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}. For any vector z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, let ‖z‖1\|z\|_{1} and ‖z‖∞\|z\|_{\infty} denote the standard ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norms, respectively. Given a collection of variables s1,…,sns_{1},\dots,s_{n} and Δ⊆[n]\Delta\subseteq[n], the shorthand sΔs_{\Delta} denotes the set {si:i∈Δ}\{s_{i}:i\in\Delta\}. We use O~​(⋅)\tilde{O}(\cdot) notation to suppress polylogarithmic factors in all problem parameters except nn. For a discrete measurable space (𝒳,ℱ)(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{F}), the total variation distance between probability measures ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} is defined as TV⁡(ρ1,ρ2)=12​∑x∈𝒳|ρ1​(x)−ρ2​(x)|\mathrm{TV}(\rho_{1},\rho_{2})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}|\rho_{1}(x)-\rho_{2}(x)|. We write x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D} to indicate that xx is sampled from the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and x∼𝒰⁡(Ω)x\sim\mathcal{U}(\Omega) to denote sampling from the uniform distribution over a finite set Ω\Omega.

Graphons. A graphon is a bounded, measurable, symmetric function W:ℐ2→ℐW\!:\!\mathcal{I}^{2}\!\to\!\mathcal{I}, where ℐ=[0,1]\mathcal{I}\!\!=\!\![0,1], that encodes interaction weights in dense graphs. Given deterministic latent points {αi}i=1n⊂[0,1]\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\!\subset\![0,1], the graphon induces a complete weighted interaction matrix with entries wi​j≔W⁡(αi,αj)w_{ij}\coloneqq W(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}) (and wi​i≔0w_{ii}\coloneqq 0). Graphons arise as limit objects for dense graphs, and any finite weighted graph GG admits an associated underlying graphon WGW_{G} constructed from its adjacency matrix (Lovász, 2012).

2.1 Problem Formulation

We consider a system of nn cooperative agents indexed by [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} denote the finite state and action spaces of each agent, respectively (Assumption 3.4). At each time tt, the agents have a joint state s⁡(t)=(s1​(t),…,sn​(t))∈𝒮ns(t)=(s_{1}(t),\dots,s_{n}(t))\in\mathcal{S}^{n} and select a joint action a⁡(t)=(a1​(t),…,an​(t))∈𝒜na(t)=(a_{1}(t),\dots,a_{n}(t))\in\mathcal{A}^{n}. The interactions between the agents can be written as a weighted graph 𝔾=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathbb{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) with vertex set 𝒱=[n]\mathcal{V}=[n], where edge weights are determined by a measurable, bounded, symmetric graphon W:ℐ2→ℐW:\mathcal{I}^{2}\to\mathcal{I} for ℐ=[0,1]\mathcal{I}=[0,1]. Each agent ii is assigned a latent coordinate αi=i/n∈ℐ\alpha_{i}=i/n\in\mathcal{I}, enabling the graphon to represent non-uniform interaction structures within the network.

Definition 2.1 (Graphon-weighted neighborhood state-action feature for agent ii).

Let W:[0,1]2→[0,1]W:[0,1]^{2}\to[0,1] be a graphon. We fix deterministic latent coordinates {αi}i=1n⊂[0,1]\{\alpha_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\subset[0,1]. The graphon induces a complete weighted interaction graph wi​j≔W⁡(αi,αj)w_{ij}\coloneqq W(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}) where wi​i≔0w_{ii}\coloneqq 0, and normalized influence weights for each ii, w¯i​j≔wi​j∑m≠iwi​m\bar{w}_{ij}\coloneqq\frac{w_{ij}}{\sum_{m\neq i}w_{im}}, where w¯i​i≔0\bar{w}_{ii}\coloneqq 0. Then, for a joint state/action pair (𝐬,𝐚)∈𝒮n×𝒜n(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a})\!\in\!\mathcal{S}^{n}\!\times\!\mathcal{A}^{n}, agent ii’s graphon-weighted neighborhood state/action feature is a probability mass function zi∈𝒵⊂𝒫⁡(𝒮×𝒜)z_{i}\in\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}), defined for all (x,u)∈𝒮×𝒜(x,u)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A},

zi​(x,u)≔∑j≠iw¯i​j​𝟙​{𝐬j=x,𝐚j=u},z_{i}(x,u)\coloneqq\sum_{j\neq i}\bar{w}_{ij}\mathbbm{1}\{\mathbf{s}_{j}=x,\mathbf{a}_{j}=u\},

where its state marginal is gzi​(x)=∑u∈𝒜zi​(x,u)∈𝒢g_{z_{i}}(x)\!=\!\sum_{u\in\mathcal{A}}z_{i}(x,u)\!\in\!\mathcal{G} and action marginal is hzi​(u)=∑x∈𝒮zi​(x,u)∈ℋh_{z_{i}}(u)\!=\!\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}}z_{i}(x,u)\!\in\!\mathcal{H}.

Agent dynamics. Let 𝔊⁡(𝒮)\mathfrak{G}(\mathcal{S}) denote the space of neighborhood state features, the probability simplex over 𝒮\mathcal{S}. At time tt, agent ii observes its local state si​(t)s_{i}(t) and its neighborhood feature. It selects an action ai​(t)∈𝒜a_{i}(t)\in\mathcal{A}, and the next state evolves according to the transition kernel P:𝒮×𝒜×𝔊⁡(𝒮)→𝒫⁡(𝒮)P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathfrak{G}(\mathcal{S})\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}), such that si(t+1)∼P(⋅∣si(t),ai(t),gi(t))s_{i}(t+1)\sim P(\cdot\mid s_{i}(t),a_{i}(t),g_{i}(t)) for all i∈[n]i\in[n], where gi​(t)∈𝔊​(𝒮)g_{i}(t)\in\mathfrak{G}(\mathcal{S}) is agent ii’s graphon-weighted neighborhood state feature. That is, the agent transitions depend only on empirical neighborhood features g∈𝔊⁡(𝒮)g\in\mathfrak{G}({\mathcal{S}}).

Team objective. We define a local reward function rℓ:𝒮×𝒜×𝔊⁡(𝒮)→ℝr_{\ell}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathfrak{G}(\mathcal{S})\to\mathbb{R} for each agent, and the team stage reward on (𝐬1:n(t),𝐚1:n(t),𝐠1:n(t))∈𝒮n×𝒜n×𝒢n(\mathbf{s}_{1:n}(t),\mathbf{a}_{1:n}(t),\mathbf{g}_{1:n}(t))\in\mathcal{S}^{n}\times\mathcal{A}^{n}\times\mathcal{G}^{n} as rtr_{t} where

Vteamπ(𝐬1:n)≔𝔼π[∑t≥0γtrt|𝐬1:n(0)=𝐬1:n].V^{\pi}_{\text{team}}(\mathbf{s}_{1:n})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}r_{t}\bigg|\mathbf{s}_{1:n}(0)=\mathbf{s}_{1:n}\right].

Note that each agent ii’s state transition and reward depends on agents [n]∖i[n]\setminus i only through the state marginal gi​(x)g_{i}(x), but the evolution of gi​(x)g_{i}(x) depends on how they choose actions based on their states, which is captured in Zi​(x,u)Z_{i}(x,u).

Definition 2.2 (ϵ\epsilon-optimal policy).

A policy π\pi is ϵ\epsilon-optimal if for all 𝐬1:n∈𝒮n\mathbf{s}_{1:n}\in\mathcal{S}^{n}, we have Vteamπ​(𝐬)≥supπ∗Vteamπ∗​(𝐬)−ϵV^{\pi}_{\text{team}}(\mathbf{s})\geq\sup_{\pi^{*}}V^{\pi^{*}}_{\text{team}}(\mathbf{s})-\epsilon.

Motivating Examples. Below we give examples of cooperative graphon MARL settings naturally captured by this formulation. Our empirical results show that the average cumulative discounted return of learned policies increases monotonically as the subsampling parameter κ\kappa approaches nn, while providing a computational speedup over graphon mean-field QQ-learning methods.11 1 We provide more details of our numerical experiments in Appendix A and have released the code here.

  • •

    Robot Coordination in Constrained Workspaces. Consider a swarm of nn mobile robots performing collaborative tasks (e.g., cargo transport in a warehouse). Since robots operate in constrained regions (aisles and loading zones), local congestion can significantly affect task completion times. If robot ii is assigned a location αi∈[0,1]2\alpha_{i}\in[0,1]^{2}, we can model their interactions with a graphon W(αi,αj)=𝟙{∥αi−αj∥2≤r}W(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j})=\mathbbm{1}\{\|\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{j}\|_{2}\leq r\} and a fixed interaction radius r>0r>0, reflecting concerns like collision avoidance, and its empirical neighborhood state-action distribution z^i(κ)\hat{z}_{i}^{(\kappa)} and its state marginal g^i(κ)\hat{g}_{i}^{(\kappa)} are used to compute its reward. For tractability, each agent constructs a κ\kappa-sampled approximation of its neighborhood aggregate via graphon-weighted subsampling, so that a robot’s optimal policy is primarily influenced by nearby agents (e.g., those sharing an aisle) rather than further ones. These heterogeneous densities can be represented with a block-structured graphon where different subsections of the unit square correspond to workspace sectors with varying congestion levels (Figure 1(a)).

  • •

    Autonomous Vehicle Coordination. Consider nn autonomous vehicles navigating a road network where efficient coordination is needed to minimize travel times and prevent gridlock. In classical mean-field settings, all agents are assumed to interact uniformly, but real-world traffic dynamics exhibit significant locality as a vehicle’s congestion experience typically depends on the density of nearby traffic rather than the state of the entire network. This spatial structure is captured by a distance-decay graphon W⁡(αi,αj)=exp⁡(−β​|αi−αj|)W(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j})=\exp(-\beta|\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{j}|), where vehicles that are close to one another exert a strong mutual influence while those further away have a negligible impact on local flow. To enable scalable learning in this environment, each vehicle could use graphon-weighted subsampling to approximate the local traffic density without having to process the full network information. This allows decentralized policies that respect the underlying locality of traffic dynamics, thereby allowing vehicles to make informed decisions to improve overall network throughput (Figure 1(b)).

Capturing heterogeneity in state/action spaces. Following Mondal et al. (2022), we model heterogeneity in agent states and actions by incorporating agent types directly into the state. Specifically, each agent ii is assigned a type εi∈ℰ\varepsilon_{i}\in\mathcal{E}, and we define the state space 𝒮=ℰ×𝒮′\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{S}^{\prime}, where ℰ\mathcal{E} indexes agent types and 𝒮′\mathcal{S}^{\prime} denotes the latent state space. The transition and reward functions may then depend explicitly on the agent’s type.

3 Graphon Mean-Field Subsampling (GMFS)

We propose Graphon Mean-Field Subsampling (GMFS), a framework that handles agent heterogeneity through non-uniform interactions modeled by graphons. To ensure scalability in large-scale systems, we introduce a subsampled neighborhood approximation, where each agent constructs an empirical neighborhood histogram from a small subset of the population. Using the graphon aggregates from Definition 2.1, GMFS learns an approximately optimal policy that achieves near-optimal team rewards under a sampled mean-field limit. This approach extends local sampling used in graph neural networks (Hamilton et al., 2017) to the MARL setting.

Assumption 3.1 (Well-defined graphon weights).

We assume the underlying graphon W:[0,1]2→[0,1]W:[0,1]^{2}\to[0,1] satisfies ∫01W⁡(α,β)​𝑑β>0for all ​α∈[0,1],\int_{0}^{1}W(\alpha,\beta)d\beta>0\quad\text{for all }\alpha\in[0,1], ensuring that all row-normalized graphon weights are well defined.

Definition 3.2 (Graphon-weighted Subsampling).

Fix κ≥1\kappa\geq 1. For each agent i∈[n]i\in[n], sample a multiset of κ\kappa neighbors Δi=(Ji(1),⋯,Ji(κ))\Delta_{i}=(J_{i}^{(1)},\cdots,J_{i}^{(\kappa)}) where Ji(m)∼w¯i,⋅J_{i}^{(m)}\sim\bar{w}_{i,\cdot} on [n]∖{i}[n]\setminus\{i\}. Across all the agents, this yields a collection {Δi}i=1n\{\Delta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}.

Definition 3.3 (Sampled neighborhood aggregates).

For κ≥1\kappa\geq 1, let 𝒢κ≔𝒫κ​(𝒮)⊂𝔊⁡(𝒮)\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}\coloneqq\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{S})\subset\mathfrak{G}(\mathcal{S}) and 𝒵κ≔𝒫κ​(𝒮×𝒜)\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}\coloneqq\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}) be the sets of empirical histograms with denominator κ\kappa. Given Δi\Delta_{i} from Definition 3.2, define the empirical κ\kappa-sample neighborhood state-action distribution Z^i(κ)∈𝒵κ\hat{Z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}\in\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}, where

Z^i(κ)​(s,a)≔1κ​∑m=1κ𝟙​{sJi(m)=s,aJi(m)=a},\hat{Z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(s,a)\coloneqq\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{J_{i}^{(m)}}=s,\ a_{J_{i}^{(m)}}=a\},

and let the sampled neighborhood state marginal g^i(κ)∈𝒢κ\hat{g}_{i}^{(\kappa)}\in\mathcal{G}_{\kappa} be given by g^i(κ)​(s)≔∑a∈𝒜Z^i(κ)​(s,a).\hat{g}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(s)\coloneqq\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\hat{Z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(s,a).

Sampled local reward. Each agent evaluates its local reward through the sampled neighborhood feature rℓ​(si,ai,g^i(κ))r_{\ell}(s_{i},a_{i},\hat{g}_{i}^{(\kappa)}) as an approximation of the true mean-field reward. The discrepancy between this sampled value and the ground truth is governed by the regularity conditions established in the following assumptions.

Assumption 3.4 (Finite state/action spaces).

We assume that the state and action spaces of all the agents in the system are finite: |𝒮|,|𝒜|<∞|\mathcal{S}|,|\mathcal{A}|<\infty. Appendix G relaxes this assumption to the non-tabular setting with infinite continuous states.

Assumption 3.5 (Bounded rewards).

We assume that the components of the reward function are bounded. Specifically, we assume ‖rℓ‖∞<∞\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}<\infty.

Assumption 3.6 (The local component of the reward function is 2​‖rℓ‖∞2\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}-Lipschitz in the empirical distribution).

We assume that for all s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A}, and g,g′∈𝔊⁡(𝒮)g,g^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{G}(\mathcal{S}),

|rℓ​(s,a,g)−rℓ​(s,a,g′)|≤2​‖rℓ‖∞⋅TV⁡(g,g′).|r_{\ell}(s,a,g)-r_{\ell}(s,a,g^{\prime})|\leq 2\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(g,g^{\prime}).
Assumption 3.7 (Transitions are LPL_{P}-Lipschitz).

There exists 1≤LP<∞1\leq L_{P}<\infty such that for all s,as,a and all g,g′∈𝔊⁡(𝒮)g,g^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{G}(\mathcal{S}),

TV(P(⋅|s,a,g),P(⋅|s,a,g′))≤LP⋅TV(g,g′).\mathrm{TV}(P(\cdot|s,a,g),P(\cdot|s,a,g^{\prime}))\leq L_{P}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(g,g^{\prime}).

For p∈{1,…,n−1}p\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}, define the Banach space 𝒴p={Q:𝒮×𝒜×𝒵p→ℝ}\mathcal{Y}_{p}\!=\!\{Q:\mathcal{S}\!\times\!\mathcal{A}\!\times\!\mathcal{Z}_{p}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}\} equipped with the sup-norm ‖Q‖∞≔sups,a,z|Q⁡(s,a,z)|\|Q\|_{\infty}\!\coloneqq\!\sup_{s,a,z}|Q(s,a,z)|.

Team value decomposition. Under the policy class where each agent’s decision rule depends only on its local observation (si,gi)(s_{i},g_{i}), the induced value function for agent ii can be written as a function of sis_{i} and gig_{i}. Then, the team value decomposes as Vteamπ(𝐬1:n,𝐠1:n)=1n∑i=1nVπ(si,gi)V_{\text{team}}^{\pi}(\mathbf{s}_{1:n},\mathbf{g}_{1:n})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}V^{\pi}(s_{i},g_{i}), which is 𝔼​[Vπ​(s,g)]\mathbb{E}[V^{\pi}(s,g)] for a uniformly random agent i∈[n]i\in[n].

Q-function. We introduce a shared QQ-function that is optimized centrally. Fix κ≥2\kappa\geq 2 and let 𝒵κ\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa} denote the discrete set of empirical joint histograms on 𝒮×𝒜\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A} with denominator κ\kappa. Let 𝒢κ≔𝒫κ​(𝒮)\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}\coloneqq\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{S}). Qπ(s,a,z)=rℓ(s,a,gz)+γ𝔼(s′,g′)∼𝒥n(⋅∣s,a,z)[Vπ(s′,g′)],\displaystyle Q^{\pi}(s,a,z)\!=\!r_{\ell}(s,a,g_{z})\!+\!\gamma\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{J}_{n}(\cdot\mid s,a,z)}\!\left[V^{\pi}\!\big(s^{\prime},g^{\prime}\big)\right],

where 𝒥n\mathcal{J}_{n} is the induced one-step kernel, for a uniformly random agent, on (s,g)(s,g) under the nn-agent dynamics,

Decentralized Execution. For g∈𝒢κg\in\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}, define the fiber Γκ​(g)≔{z∈𝒵κ:gz=g}\Gamma_{\kappa}(g)\coloneqq\{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}:\ g_{z}=g\} and the Bellman backup given by ℳκ​Q​(s,g)≔maxa∈𝒜,z∈Γκ​(g)⁡Q⁡(s,a,z)\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}Q(s,g)\coloneqq\max_{a\in\mathcal{A},z\in\Gamma_{\kappa}(g)}Q(s,a,z). The neighborhood histogram zz is a latent variable generated by the environment and determined by the other agents’ states and actions. It is not a directly controllable parameter for individual agents. Thus the maximization over zz is not an action choice, but used as an optimization over latent variables to define a value function on (s,g)(s,g) that upper-bounds achievable returns under under all completions consistent with gg. The optimal (greedy) policy therefore selects an action

π∗(⋅∣s,g)∈ℳκQ∗(s,g)=argmaxa∈𝒜,z∈Γκ​(g)Q∗(s,a,z),\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid s,g)\in\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}Q^{*}(s,g)=\arg\!\!\!\max_{a\in\mathcal{A},z\in\Gamma_{\kappa}(g)}Q^{*}(s,a,z),

with the maximization over zz serving to evaluate the action under the most favorable compatible neighborhood realization. In the fully centralized setting, optimal control would involve coordinating actions across all agents, which jointly determine the resulting neighborhood aggregate. During decentralized execution however, agents execute only the local action component and do not attempt to control or realize any particular completion zz.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the Bellman operator, where we then apply the Bellman update iteratively on each agent’s Q-function. Execution is decentralized since each agent is able to locally construct an estimate z^i(κ)\hat{z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}. Thus, rewards and transitions depend on neighbors only through the neighborhood state marginal gzg_{z}, enabling each agent to optimize using local observations without knowing explicit identity information.

Definition 3.8 (Bellman operator 𝒯\mathcal{T}).

For Q∈𝒴n−1Q\in\mathcal{Y}_{n-1}, define

𝒯​Q​(s,a,z)\displaystyle\mathcal{T}Q(s,a,z)\! ≔rℓ​(s,a,gz)\displaystyle\coloneqq\!r_{\ell}(s,a,g_{z})
+γ𝔼(s′,g′)∼𝒥n(⋅∣s,a,z)[ℳn−1Q(s′,g′)],\displaystyle+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{J}_{n}(\cdot\mid s,a,z)}[\mathcal{M}_{n-1}Q(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})],

where 𝒥n(⋅|s,a,z)\mathcal{J}_{n}(\cdot|s,a,z) is the induced one-step kernel on (s′,g′)(s^{\prime},g^{\prime}) under the nn-agent dynamics, for a uniformly random agent.

Definition 3.9 (Sampled Bellman operator 𝒯^κ\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}).

For Q^κ∈𝒴κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa}\in\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa}, define

𝒯^κ​Q^κ​(s,a,z)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}\hat{Q}_{\kappa}(s,a,z) ≔rℓ​(s,a,gz)\displaystyle\coloneqq r_{\ell}(s,a,g_{z})
+γ𝔼(s′,g′)∼𝒥κ(⋅∣s,a,z)[ℳκQ^κ(s′,g′)],\displaystyle+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}(\cdot\mid s,a,z)}[\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}\hat{Q}_{\kappa}(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})],

where 𝒥κ(⋅∣s,a,z)\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}(\cdot\mid s,a,z) is the induced one-step kernel on (s′,g′)(s^{\prime},g^{\prime}) generated by the (κ+1)(\kappa+1)-agent surrogate dynamics, for a uniformly random agent.

Definition 3.10 (Empirical sampled operator 𝒯^κ,m\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}).

Given m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, let (sℓ′,gℓ′)ℓ=1m(s^{\prime}_{\ell},g^{\prime}_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{m} be i.i.d. samples from 𝒥κ(⋅∣s,a,z)\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}(\cdot\mid s,a,z). Then, define

𝒯^κ,m​Q^κ,m​(s,a,z)≔rℓ​(s,a,gz)+γm​∑ℓ=1mℳκ​Q^κ,m​(sℓ′,gℓ′).\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}(s,a,z)\!\coloneqq\!r_{\ell}(s,a,g_{z})+\frac{\gamma}{m}\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}(s^{\prime}_{\ell},g_{\ell}^{\prime}).

As a centralized-training decentralized-execution framework, GMFS proceeds as follows. First, Algorithm 1 uses a generative oracle to derive an optimal QQ-function on a (κ+1)(\kappa+1)-agent surrogate model. Learning on this restricted subspace yields a policy governed by the subsampling parameter κ\kappa instead of the total population size nn. Subsequently, Algorithm 2 describes how agents deploy this learned policy in a decentralized environment. During execution, each agent ii independently approximates its neighborhood marginal g^i(κ)\hat{g}_{i}^{(\kappa)} by sampling κ\kappa neighbors based on the graphon weights. This ensures that the computational cost per agent is independent of nn, enabling scalable coordination in large-scale heterogeneous systems.

4 Theoretical Guarantees and Analysis

We establish theoretical guarantees for GMFS by analyzing approximation errors due to neighborhood subsampling and finite-sample estimation. We define the properties of the sampled Bellman operators, and provide optimality bounds for the learned policy as a function of κ\kappa and mm.

Bellman noise. We introduce the Bellman noise, ϵκ,m\epsilon_{\kappa,m}, to account for the error in estimating the operator from finite samples. The empirical operator 𝒯^κ,m\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m} is an unbiased estimator of the sampled Bellman operator 𝒯^κ\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}. As shown in Lemma B.4, both 𝒯^κ\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa} and 𝒯^κ,m\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m} are γ\gamma-contractions with fixed-points Q^κ∗\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*} and Q^κ,m∗\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{*} respectively. By the law of large numbers, limm→∞𝒯^κ,m=𝒯^κ\smash{\lim_{m\to\infty}\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}=\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}} and ‖Q^κ,m∗−Q^κ∗‖∞→0\smash{\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{*}-\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}\|_{\infty}\to 0} as m→∞m\to\infty. For finite mm, we define this discrepancy as ϵκ,m≔‖Q^κ,m∗−Q^κ∗‖∞\epsilon_{\kappa,m}\coloneq\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{*}-\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}\|_{\infty}.

Sample complexity and optimality. The efficiency of GMFS is reflected in its sample complexity. For a fixed κ\kappa, Algorithm 1 learns π^kest\hat{\pi}^{\mathrm{est}}_{k} with an asymptotic sample complexity of O~​(κ|𝒮|​|𝒜|​|𝒮|2​|𝒜|2)\tilde{O}(\kappa^{|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|}|\mathcal{S}|^{2}|\mathcal{A}|^{2}), which is at least polynomially faster than standard QQ-learning or mean-field value iteration. As shown in Theorem 4.1, the optimality gap decays as κ→n\kappa\to n, which reveals a fundamental trade-off: increasing κ\kappa improves policy performance but increases the size of the QQ-function. If we set κ=O⁡(log⁡n)\kappa=O(\log n), the complexity becomes O~​((log⁡n)|𝒮|​|𝒜|​|𝒮|2​|𝒜|2)\tilde{O}((\log n)^{|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|}|\mathcal{S}|^{2}|\mathcal{A}|^{2}). This is an exponential speedup over the complexity of mean-field value iteration, from poly⁡(n)\mathrm{poly}(n) to poly⁡(log⁡n)\mathrm{poly}(\log n), as well as over traditional value-iteration, where the optimality gap decays at a rate of O⁡(1log⁡n)O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log n}}).

There is evidence suggesting that the optimality gap of O~​(1/κ)\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{\kappa}) is sharp. An obstacle to improving this bound is the known optimal error of O~​(1/n)\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n}) in standard mean-field MARL. The algorithmic bottleneck in achieving a faster rate than O~​(1/κ)\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{\kappa}) comes from learning the Q^κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa} function rather than the online execution strategy. When κ=n−1\kappa=n-1, GMFS reduces to mean-field learning with a rate of O~​(1/n)\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n}), which matches the tight bound by Yang et al. (2018). This illustrates a natural difficulty in improving the rate and provides evidence for why our bound is tight.

The poly⁡(11−γ)\mathrm{poly}(\frac{1}{1-\gamma})-dependence in our results may be loose because we do not use more complicated variance reduction techniques as in (Sidford et al., 2018a; Sidford et al., 2018b; Wainwright, 2019; Jin et al., 2024) to optimize the number of samples mm used to bound the Bellman error ϵκ,m\epsilon_{\kappa,m}. Incorporating variance reduction would significantly increase the complexity of the algorithm and the underlying intuition. Finally, the GMFS formulation extends to off-policy QQ-learning (Chen et al., 2021b), which replaces the generative oracle with a stochastic approximation scheme to learn from historical data. This extension is detailed in Appendix F, where we provide theoretical guarantees with a similar decaying optimality gap.

Generalization to infinite state spaces. In non-tabular environments with infinite state and action spaces, value-based RL methods can use function approximation to learn Q^κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa} via deep QQ-networks (Silver et al., 2016). This introduces an additional error term in the performance bound of Theorem 4.1, which we analyze under a Linear MDP structure.

Assumption 4.4 (Linear MDP with infinite state spaces).

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be an infinite compact set, and assume a feature map ϕ:𝒮×𝒜×𝒵→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, dd unknown (signed) measures μ=(μ1,…,μd)\mu=(\mu^{1},\dots,\mu^{d}) over 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and a vector θ∈ℝd\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that for any (s,a,z)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒵(s,a,z)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Z}, we have ℙ(⋅|s,a,z)=⟨ϕ(s,a,z),μ(⋅)⟩\mathbb{P}(\cdot|s,a,z)=\langle\phi(s,a,z),\mu(\cdot)\rangle and r⁡(s,a,gz)=⟨ϕ⁡(s,a,z),θ⟩r(s,a,g_{z})=\langle\phi(s,a,z),\theta\rangle.

The existence of ϕ\phi implies one can estimate the QQ-function of any policy as a linear function. This assumption is used in policy iteration methods (Lattimore et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023), and we exploit it to obtain sample complexity bounds independently of |𝒮||\mathcal{S}| and |𝒜||\mathcal{A}|. As is standard in RL, we assume bounded feature-norms (Tkachuk et al., 2023):

Assumption 4.5 (Bounded features).

We assume that ‖ϕ⁡(s,a,z)‖2≤1\|\phi(s,a,z)\|_{2}\leq 1 for all (s,a,z)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒵(s,a,z)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Z}.

Following the reduction from Zhang et al. (2024b); Ren et al. (2025), we use function approximation to learn spectral features ϕκ\phi_{\kappa} for Q^κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa}. We derive a performance guarantee for the learned policy πκest\pi_{\kappa}^{\mathrm{est}}, where the optimality gap decays with κ\kappa.

When πκest{\pi}^{\mathrm{est}}_{\kappa} is derived from the spectral features ϕκ\phi_{\kappa} learned in Q^κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa}, and MM is the number of samples used in the function approximation, then with probability at least 1−150​κ−201100​κ1-\frac{1}{50\kappa}-\frac{201}{100\sqrt{\kappa}}, we have

≤O~​(d+|𝒜|κ+dM+2​LP​γ​‖rℓ‖∞κ).\displaystyle\leq\!\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{d\!+\!|\mathcal{A}|}{\kappa}}\!+\!\frac{d}{\sqrt{M}}\!+\!\frac{2L_{P}\gamma\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\right).

Although dM\frac{d}{\sqrt{M}} grows linearly with the dimension, it is controlled by the sample budget MM (i.e., chosen to scale with κ\kappa, e.g., M≳κ2​d2M\gtrsim\kappa^{2}d^{2}) so that it remains lower order relative to the O~​(1/κ)\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{\kappa}) terms. 5 Proof Outline

In this section, we provide an outline of the derivation for our main results through three steps: (1) proving Lipschitz stability of the Bellman iterates, (2) bounding subsampling error via concentration inequalities, and (3) establishing a global performance guarantee using the performance difference lemma. See Appendices C and D.

Step 1: Lipschitz Continuity. We compare the QQ-function evaluated under two neighborhood aggregates z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} and z^∈𝒵κ\hat{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}, whose state marginals gzg_{z} and gz^g_{\hat{z}} differ in total variation. Specifically, we show:

Theorem 5.1 (Lipschitz Continuity of the Bellman iterates).

Fix a subsampling parameter κ≥1\kappa\geq 1. Fix (s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}, and let z∈𝒵≔Δ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)z\in\mathcal{Z}\coloneqq\Delta(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}). Let z^∈𝒵κ\hat{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa} be the empirical histogram of κ\kappa i.i.d. draws from zz, and let gz,gz^g_{z},g_{\hat{z}} be the marginals in 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Then, for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, we have

|Qt​(s,a,z)−Q^κt​(s,a,z^)|≤4​‖rℓ‖∞1−γ​LP⋅TV⁡(gz,gz^).\displaystyle\left|Q^{t}(s,a,z)-\hat{Q}^{t}_{\kappa}(s,a,\hat{z})\right|\leq\frac{4\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}L_{P}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(g_{z},g_{\hat{z}}).

We defer the full proof of Theorem 5.1 to Appendix C.

Step 2: Concentration of the Subsampled Mean-Field. Next, we bound the discrepancy between the κ\kappa-sampled aggregate g^i(κ)\hat{g}_{i}^{(\kappa)} and the true graphon-weighted mean-field gig_{i}. We establish a concentration inequality for empirical distributions drawn from a finite population to show that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta:

|Qt​(s,a,z)−Q^κt​(s,a,z^)|≤4​LP​‖rℓ‖∞1−γ​|𝒮|​ln+ln⁡2δ2​κ.\left|Q^{t}(s,a,z)\!-\!\hat{Q}^{t}_{\kappa}(s,a,\hat{z})\right|\!\leq\!\frac{4L_{P}\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}\!\sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal{S}|\ln 2\!+\!\ln\frac{2}{\delta}}{2\kappa}}.

This result introduces the O⁡(1/κ)O(1/\sqrt{\kappa}) rate; the proof is provided in Appendix C.1.

Step 3: Performance Difference. Finally, we combine the previous steps to bound the performance gap between the learned policy πκest\pi_{\kappa}^{\mathrm{est}} from GMFS and the optimal policy π∗\pi^{*}. Using Lemma D.6, we obtain a uniform bound on the optimality of the estimated joint policy in terms of the discrepancy between Q∗Q^{*} and Q^κ∗\hat{Q}^{*}_{\kappa}. We also account for the additional error introduced by finite-sample Bellman noise εκ,m\varepsilon_{\kappa,m}. This allows us to apply the performance difference lemma (Kakade and Langford, 2002), yielding Theorem 4.3. The full proof is provided in Appendix D.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we consider the problem of learning an optimal policy in a cooperative system of nn heterogeneous agents. We propose an algorithm, GMFS, which derives a policy π~κest\tilde{\pi}_{\kappa}^{\mathrm{est}} where κ≤n\kappa\leq n is a tunable parameter for the number of agents sampled. We show that π~κest\tilde{\pi}_{\kappa}^{\mathrm{est}} converges to the optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} with a decay rate of O⁡(1/κ)O(1/\sqrt{\kappa}). To establish this result, we develop an adapted Bellman operator 𝒯^κ\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa} and prove its contraction property. The key technical novelty of this work lies in proving a Lipschitz continuity result for Q^κ∗\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*} and leveraging the weights of a corresponding graphon. Finally, we supplement our theoretical results with motivating examples and provide additional empirical validation (see Appendix A.4) via numerical simulations of robotic control.

Limitations and Future Work. While GMFS is a scalable framework for heterogeneous MARL, there are several areas for extending its theoretical and practical scope. For instance, a natural next step is to derive matching lower bounds to demonstrate the tightness of our analysis for subsampling in graphon-weighted systems. Our analysis assumes access to a generative simulator; extending GMFS to a purely online setting with streaming interaction data and exploration-exploitation trade-offs would extend its applicability to model-free environments. It would also be interesting to study higher-order interaction structures, such as Markov random fields or hypergraph-based mean-fields, to capture context-dependent heterogeneity (Wang et al., 2026). Another direction would be to examine whether online mirror descent can be integrated with our algorithm, as in Fabian et al. (2023), to get better numerical stability. Finally, it would be interesting to adapt GMFS beyond cooperative MARL to mixed cooperative-competitive environments or federated learning with non-uniform communication.

Impact Statement

This paper advances the field of machine learning by enabling more principled design and analysis of large-scale systems. Potential applications include autonomous driving, robotics, and other cooperative control settings. We believe these improvements will have a positive impact on society by improving the efficiency of autonomous infrastructure.

Outline of the Appendices.

  • •

    Section A provides our numerical simulations, experimental details, and supplemental examples;

  • •

    Section B provides mathematical background, and relevant introductory lemmas;

  • •

    Section C presents the proof of the Lipschitz continuity of the QQ-function in the mean-field measure;

  • •

    Section D bounds the optimality gap between the learned stochastic policy and the optimal policy;

  • •

    Section E extends the result to stochastic rewards;

  • •

    Section F extends the result to off-policy learning;

  • •

    Section G extends the result to continuous state spaces.

Appendix A Numerical Simulations and Additional Motivating Examples

In this section, we provide an additional conceptual formulation of GMFS within the context of smart grid management. We then provide an empirical evaluation of the algorithm using a cooperative robotics coordination task.

A.1 Motivating Example: Cooperative Autonomous Driving

Consider a population of nn autonomous vehicles indexed by i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}. Each agent ii is associated with a latent feature αi∈[0,1]\alpha_{i}\in[0,1] representing its position along a road segment. Interactions are governed by a graphon W:[0,1]2→[0,1]W:[0,1]^{2}\to[0,1], where W⁡(αi,αj)W(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}) represents the strength of the interaction between vehicles indexed by ii and jj. For example, we model distance-decaying influence along the road with: W⁡(αi,αj)=exp⁡(−β​|αi−αj|)W(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j})=\exp(-\beta|\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{j}|). Each agent has state si∈𝒮s_{i}\in\mathcal{S}, which can encode the position or velocity, and selects actions ai∈𝒜a_{i}\in\mathcal{A}, which can include steering and acceleration. Vehicle ii transitions according si(t+1)∼P(⋅∣si(t),ai(t),gi(t))s_{i}(t+1)\sim P\big(\cdot\mid s_{i}(t),a_{i}(t),g_{i}(t)\big). At each time tt, vehicle ii constructs a multiset of κ\kappa neighbors Δi​(t)=(Ji(1)​(t),…,Ji(κ)​(t))\Delta_{i}(t)=(J_{i}^{(1)}(t),\dots,J_{i}^{(\kappa)}(t)) and forms the empirical histograms:

Z^i(κ)​(t)​(s,a)\displaystyle\hat{Z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(t)(s,a) =1κ​∑m=1κ{sJi(m)​(t)​(t)=s,aJi(m)​(t)​(t)=a},\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\mathbbm{1}\!\left\{s_{J_{i}^{(m)}(t)}(t)=s,a_{J_{i}^{(m)}(t)}(t)=a\right\},
g^i(κ)​(t)​(s)\displaystyle\hat{g}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(t)(s) =∑a∈𝒜Z^i(κ)​(t)​(s,a).\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\hat{Z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(t)(s,a).

Since the distance-decay graphon induces decaying weights, the dominant contributors in this example to gi​(t)g_{i}(t) are the nearby vehicles. Thus, sampling from w¯i​j\bar{w}_{ij} targets the most informative neighbors. Increasing κ\kappa tightens concentration of g^i(κ)​(t)\hat{g}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(t) while keeping the per-agent computation scalable.

A.2 Motivating Example: Cooperative Robot Coordination Task

Consider nn mobile robots indexed by i∈[n]i\in[n] operating in a warehouse. Associate each robot with a latent coordinate αi∈[0,1]\alpha_{i}\in[0,1] capturing its location along an embedding of aisles/loading zones. Let W:[0,1]2→[0,1]W:[0,1]^{2}\to[0,1] encode interaction intensity. We consider a radius graphon W(α,β)=𝟙{|α−β|≤r}W(\alpha,\beta)=\mathbbm{1}\{|\alpha-\beta|\leq r\} for some r>0r>0, so that robots primarily interact with others in nearby regions. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a finite state space encoding each robot’s local mode and task-relevant information, such as idle, moving, standing. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a finite action space which includes move, wait, pickup. At time tt, robot ii observes its local state si​(t)s_{i}(t) and a neighborhood summary, selects an action ai​(t)∈𝒜a_{i}(t)\in\mathcal{A}, and transitions according to si(t+1)∼P(⋅∣si(t),ai(t),gi(t))s_{i}(t+1)\sim P\big(\cdot\mid s_{i}(t),a_{i}(t),g_{i}(t)\big) where gi​(t)g_{i}(t) is the graphon-weighted neighborhood state feature. In decentralized execution, robot ii does not enumerate all neighbors. The sampled local reward is evaluated as rℓ​(si​(t),ai​(t),g^i(κ)​(t))r_{\ell}(s_{i}(t),a_{i}(t),\hat{g}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(t)), capturing congestion/collision-risk effects induced by nearby robots. The interaction locality implies that the most relevant information for robot ii is concentrated among a small subset of agents with large weights w¯i​j\bar{w}_{ij}. Graphon-weighted subsampling therefore preserves the dominant neighborhood statistics while keeping per-agent computation independent of nn.

A.3 Motivating Example: Energy Distribution for a Smart Grid

Modern smart grids present a natural application for GMFS due to their high topological heterogeneity and decentralized nature. Unlike traditional power systems, a substation’s demand response in a smart grid is heavily influenced by immediate topological neighbors and local transmission constraints rather than the global average of the entire grid. In this conceptual setting, we consider nn agents representing local substations, or energy consumers, indexed by i∈[n]i\in[n].

One could model this environment by labeling each agent with a latent position αi∈[0,1]\alpha_{i}\in[0,1], which represents geographical coordinates or a position within an infrastructural hierarchy. The interaction graphon W:[0,1]2→[0,1]W:[0,1]^{2}\to[0,1] would encode the transmission efficiency and physical connectivity between substations. As noted by Singh et al. (2025), renewable energy integration requires minimizing transmission losses, which are inherently non-uniform. A graphon structure would capture this by assigning higher weights to substation pairs with high-capacity links or proximity. To ensure the resulting neighborhood sampling distribution is well-defined, we assume ∫01W⁡(α,β)​𝑑β>0\int_{0}^{1}W(\alpha,\beta)d\beta>0 for all α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], ensuring every node has a non-zero interaction density.

Under this formulation, each agent ii maintains a state si∈𝒮s_{i}\in\mathcal{S} representing its current load or energy deficit and selects an action ai∈𝒜a_{i}\in\mathcal{A} to request a specific allocation from a shared supply. At each step, agent ii would reconstruct a graphon-weighted subsampled aggregate zi∈𝒵κz_{i}\in\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa} (Def. 3.3). The reward function rℓ​(si,ai,gi)r_{\ell}(s_{i},a_{i},g_{i}) can be designed to penalize “over-allocation” costs and transmission line heating, which are non-linear functions of the local demand density. Ultimately, this example shows how GMFS could enable substations to make near-optimal allocation decisions by observing only κ≪n\kappa\ll n neighboring nodes, which avoids the need for a centralized controller to process the state of the entire national grid.

A.4 Evaluation on Cooperative Robot Coordination Task

We evaluate the empirical performance of GMFS on a cooperative robot coordination task in A.2 within a spatially constrained warehouse environment. This domain is a natural fit for graphon models because robot interactions are inherently local; a robot is significantly more affected by collision risks or blocked aisles in its immediate vicinity than by the status of a robot on the opposite side of a facility.

A key difficulty in such systems is the perception-action gap, where agents must make decisions based on incomplete social information. In Figure 4, we visualize the time-evolution of an agent’s perception. At low κ\kappa, the agent’s view of its neighborhood is sparse and noisy, resulting in high-variance estimates of local congestion. As κ\kappa increases, the agent’s empirical measure g^i\hat{g}_{i} converges to the true geometric ball defined by the graphon. In Figure 3(a), we demonstrate that GMFS allows agents to achieve near-optimal coordination even when sampling only a small fraction of the total population.

A.4.1 Experimental Setup

Environment. The robotics environment consists of n=25n=25 agents initialized on a fixed 5×55\times 5 spatial initialization grid (GG) within a unit square [0,1]2[0,1]^{2}. The agents operate within a state space 𝒮={0,1,2}\mathcal{S}=\{0,1,2\} and an action space 𝒜={0,1,2}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1,2\}, corresponding to idle (0), transit (1), and working (2) states. Actions represent the agent’s intended next state. Each evaluation run is conducted over a horizon of H=100H=100 time steps.

Compute. Experiments were implemented in Python and ran on a high-performance computing node with Intel CPUs and 1.0 TiB of DDR5 ECC RAM. We parallelized the training across subsampling parameters; the total suite took approximately 20 minutes to execute, with the exhaustive mean-field limit (κ=24\kappa=24) requiring approximately 440 seconds for training.

A.4.2 Dynamics and Rewards

We define the interaction topology using a radial graphon W⁡(x,y)W(x,y) connecting agents based on their fixed latent positions αi,αj∈[0,1]2\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\in[0,1]^{2}: W⁡(αi,αj)=𝟙​(‖αi−αj‖2≤r),W(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j})=\mathbbm{1}(\|\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{j}\|_{2}\leq r), with an interaction radius r=0.3r=0.3. We row-normalize these weights to induce the sampling distribution w¯i​j=Wi​j/∑l≠iWi​l\bar{w}_{ij}=W_{ij}/\sum_{l\neq i}W_{il}. To handle the edge case of an isolated agent (where the row sum is zero), we define w¯i​j\bar{w}_{ij} as the uniform distribution over all other agents [n]∖{i}[n]\setminus\{i\}.

The stochastic transition kernel P⁡(s′∣s,a,μ)P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a,\mu) simulates physical bottlenecks by making transitions to the working state (a=2a=2) congestion-dependent; the success probability is defined as P⁡(s′=2∣a=2,μ)=max⁡(0.1,0.9−0.8⋅μ⁡(2))P(s^{\prime}=2\mid a=2,\mu)=\max(0.1,0.9-0.8\cdot\mu(2)), with failures reverting the agent to the transit state (s′=1s^{\prime}=1). For all other actions (a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}), the agent successfully transitions to the intended state with probability 0.9, i.e., P⁡(s′=a∣a,μ)=0.9P(s^{\prime}=a\mid a,\mu)=0.9 and with a 0.1 probability of failure leaving the agent’s state unchanged (s′=ss^{\prime}=s).

To satisfy the Lipschitz and positive rewards assumptions in our framework, we define the reward function as:

r⁡(s,a,μ)=V⁡(s)⋅max⁡(0.4,1.0−L⋅μ⁡(2))−C⁡(a).r(s,a,\mu)=V(s)\cdot\max(0.4,1.0-L\cdot\mu(2))-C(a). (1)

The state values V⁡(s)V(s) are set to 10, 5, and 20 for the idle, transit, and working states, respectively. Action costs C⁡(a)C(a) are 0 for idle and transit and 5.0 for the working state. We set the congestion sensitivity to L=5.0L=5.0 with a minimum utility multiplier of 0.4.

A.4.3 GMFS Algorithm Configuration

We learn the optimal QQ-function using offline value iteration as described. In order to maintain computational tractability for large κ\kappa, we use the state-marginal histograms, which reduces the neighborhood state space 𝒵κ\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa} from (κ+88)\binom{\kappa+8}{8} (joint) to (κ+22)\binom{\kappa+2}{2} (marginal) states. This is because the environment’s rewards and transitions depend only on the neighborhood state marginal μ\mu, so the state-marginal histogram is a sufficient statistic for the optimal QQ-function in this setting. We check convergence using the Bellman error Δ=‖Qt+1−Qt‖∞\Delta=\|Q_{t+1}-Q_{t}\|_{\infty} and find that all runs reach a stable fixed point (Δ<10−4\Delta<10^{-4}) in 250 iterations. The hyperparameters used are detailed in Table 1.

Appendix B Mathematical Background and Additional Remarks

In this section, we focus on the mathematical foundations and auxiliary results required for our analysis. We first establish the contraction properties and uniform boundedness of the Bellman operators to ensure the existence and uniqueness of the optimal QQ-functions. We also present an identity-aware sampling algorithm to contrast the efficiency of our mean-field reparameterization against an exhaustive labeled state representation.

Definition B.1 (Lipschitz continuity).

Given metric spaces (𝒳,d1)(\mathcal{X},d_{1}) and (𝒴,d2)(\mathcal{Y},d_{2}) and a constant L>0L>0, a map f:𝒳→𝒴f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} is LL-Lipschitz continuous if for all x,y∈𝒳,d2​(f⁡(x),f⁡(y))≤L​d1​(x,y)x,y\in\mathcal{X},d_{2}(f(x),f(y))\leq Ld_{1}(x,y).

Theorem B.2.

(Banach-Caccioppoli Fixed Point Theorem (Banach, 1922)). Let (X,d)(X,d) be a non-empty complete metric space with a γ\gamma-contraction mapping T:X→XT:X\to X for γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Then, TT admits a unique fixed point x∗∈Xx^{*}\in X such that T⁡(x∗)=x∗T(x^{*})=x^{*}. Moreover, for any x0∈Xx_{0}\in X, Tn​(x0)→x∗T^{n}(x_{0})\to x^{*} as n→∞n\to\infty.

Lemma B.3 (The Bellman operator and sampled Bellman operator are γ\gamma-contractions).

Fix 1≤κ≤n−11\leq\kappa\leq n-1. Let 𝒴κ≔{Q:𝒮×𝒜×𝒵κ→ℝ}\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa}\coloneqq\{Q:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}\to\mathbb{R}\} be equipped with the sup norm ‖Q‖∞≔sup(s,a,z)|Q⁡(s,a,z)|\|Q\|_{\infty}\coloneqq\sup_{(s,a,z)}|Q(s,a,z)|. Suppose γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Then the Bellman operator 𝒯^κ:𝒴κ→𝒴κ\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}:\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa}\to\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa} admits a unique fixed point Q∗Q^{*} satisfying 𝒯^κ​Q∗=Q∗\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}Q^{*}=Q^{*}.

Proof.

We show that 𝒯^κ\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa} is a γ\gamma-contraction such that for all Q1,Q2∈𝒴κQ_{1},Q_{2}\in\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa}, ‖𝒯^κ​Q1−𝒯^κ​Q2‖∞≤γ​‖Q1−Q2‖∞\|\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}Q_{1}-\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}Q_{2}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma\|Q_{1}-Q_{2}\|_{\infty}. Fix any Q1,Q2∈𝒴κQ_{1},Q_{2}\in\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa} and any (s,a,z)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒵κ(s,a,z)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}, we have

|𝒯^κQ1(s,a,z)\displaystyle|\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}Q_{1}(s,a,z) −𝒯^κQ2(s,a,z)|\displaystyle-\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}Q_{2}(s,a,z)|
=|rℓ(s,a,gz)+γ𝔼(s′,g′)∼𝒥κ(⋅∣s,a,z)[ℳκQ1(s′,g′)]−rℓ(s,a,gz)−γ𝔼(s′,g′)∼𝒥κ(⋅∣s,a,z)[ℳκQ2(s′,g′)]|\displaystyle=\left|r_{\ell}(s,a,g_{z})+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}(\cdot\mid s,a,z)}[\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}Q_{1}(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})]-r_{\ell}(s,a,g_{z})-\gamma\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}(\cdot\mid s,a,z)}[\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}Q_{2}(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})]\right|
=|γ​𝔼(s′,g′)​[maxa′∈𝒜,z′∈Γκ​(g′)⁡Q1​(s′,a′,z′)]−γ​𝔼(s′,g′)​[maxa′∈𝒜,z′∈Γκ​(g′)⁡Q2​(s′,a′,z′)]|\displaystyle=\left|\gamma\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\end{subarray}}\left[\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A},z^{\prime}\in\Gamma_{\kappa}(g^{\prime})\end{subarray}}Q_{1}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},z^{\prime})\right]-\gamma\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\end{subarray}}\left[\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A},z^{\prime}\in\Gamma_{\kappa}(g^{\prime})\end{subarray}}Q_{2}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},z^{\prime})\right]\right|
≤γ​𝔼(s′,g′)​|maxa′∈𝒜,z′∈Γκ​(g′)⁡Q1​(s′,a′,z′)−maxa′∈𝒜,z′∈Γκ​(g′)⁡Q2​(s′,a′,z′)|\displaystyle\leq\gamma\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\end{subarray}}\left|\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A},z^{\prime}\in\Gamma_{\kappa}(g^{\prime})\end{subarray}}Q_{1}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},z^{\prime})-\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A},z^{\prime}\in\Gamma_{\kappa}(g^{\prime})\end{subarray}}Q_{2}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},z^{\prime})\right|
≤γ​‖Q1−Q2‖∞,\displaystyle\leq\gamma\|Q_{1}-Q_{2}\|_{\infty},

where the the third line follows by Jensen’s inequality, and the last line follows by the 11-Lipschitzness of the max operator under ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norm. Taking the supremum over (s,a,z)(s,a,z) yields ‖𝒯^κ​Q1−𝒯^κ​Q2‖∞≤γ​‖Q1−Q2‖∞\|\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}Q_{1}-\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}Q_{2}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma\|Q_{1}-Q_{2}\|_{\infty}. Since (𝒴κ,∥⋅∥∞)(\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}) is complete, Banach’s fixed point theorem implies that 𝒯κ^\hat{\mathcal{T}_{\kappa}} has a unique fixed point. The result follows for the original Bellman operator by taking κ=n−1\kappa=n-1, where 𝒯^n−1=𝒯\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{n-1}=\mathcal{T}. ∎

Lemma B.4 (The empirical sampled Bellman operator is a γ\gamma-contraction).

Fix 1≤κ≤n−11\leq\kappa\leq n-1. Let 𝒴κ≔{Q:𝒮×𝒜×𝒵κ→ℝ}\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa}\coloneqq\{Q:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}\to\mathbb{R}\} be equipped with the sup norm ‖Q‖∞≔sup(s,a,z)|Q⁡(s,a,z)|\|Q\|_{\infty}\coloneqq\sup_{(s,a,z)}|Q(s,a,z)|. Suppose γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Then the sampled Bellman operator 𝒯^κ,m:𝒴κ→𝒴κ\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}:\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa}\to\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa} admits a unique fixed point Q∗Q^{*} satisfying 𝒯^κ,m​Q^κ,m∗=Q^κ,m∗\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{*}=\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{*}.

Proof.

We show that 𝒯^κ,m\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m} is a γ\gamma-contraction such that for all Q1,Q2∈𝒴κQ_{1},Q_{2}\in\mathcal{Y}_{\kappa}, ‖𝒯^κ,m​Q1−𝒯^κ,m​Q2‖∞≤γ​‖Q1−Q2‖∞\|\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}Q_{1}-\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}Q_{2}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma\|Q_{1}-Q_{2}\|_{\infty}. =|rℓ​(s,a,gz)+γm​∑ℓ=1mℳκ​Q1​(s′,g′)−rℓ​(s,a,gz)−γm​∑ℓ=1mℳκ​Q2​(s′,g′)|\displaystyle=\left|r_{\ell}(s,a,g_{z})+\frac{\gamma}{m}\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}Q_{1}(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})-r_{\ell}(s,a,g_{z})-\frac{\gamma}{m}\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}Q_{2}(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\right|

where the the second line follows by triangle inequality, and the last line follows by the 11-Lipschitzness of the max operator under ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-norm. Taking the supremum over (s,a,z)(s,a,z) yields ‖𝒯^κ,m​Q1−𝒯^κ,m​Q2‖∞≤γ​‖Q1−Q2‖∞\|\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}Q_{1}-\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}Q_{2}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma\|Q_{1}-Q_{2}\|_{\infty}. We next show that the QQ-function is bounded throughout its iterations.

Lemma B.5.

For all T≥0T\geq 0, ‖QT‖∞≤‖r‖∞1−γ\|Q^{T}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\|r\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}.

Proof.

The proof follows by induction on TT. The base case follows as Q0≔0Q^{0}\coloneqq 0. For the induction, note that by triangle inequality ‖QT+1‖∞≤‖rℓ‖∞+γ​‖QT‖∞≤‖rℓ‖∞+γ​‖rℓ‖∞1−γ=‖rℓ‖∞1−γ\|Q^{T+1}\|_{\infty}\leq\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}+\gamma\|Q^{T}\|_{\infty}\leq\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}+\gamma\frac{\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}=\frac{\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}, which proves the claim.∎

Corollary B.6.

Observe by recursively using the γ\gamma-contractive property for TT time steps, with the initializations Q^κ=0\hat{Q}_{\kappa}=0 and Q^κ,m=0\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}=0, and the bounds ‖Q^κ∗‖∞≤‖rℓ‖∞1−γ\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\|{r}_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma} and ‖Q^κ,m∗‖∞≤‖rℓ‖∞1−γ\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\|{r}_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma} from Lemma B.5, that

‖Q^κ∗−Q^κT‖∞≤γT⋅‖Q^κ∗−Q^κ0‖∞≤γT​‖rℓ‖∞1−γ,\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}-\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{T}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma^{T}\cdot\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}-\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{0}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma^{T}\frac{\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}, (2)

and

‖Q^κ,m∗−Q^κ,mT‖∞≤γT⋅‖Q^κ,m∗−Q^κ,m0‖∞≤γT​‖rℓ‖∞1−γ.\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{*}-\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{T}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma^{T}\cdot\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{*}-\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{0}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma^{T}\frac{\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}.\\ (3)
Remark B.7.

Corollary B.6 characterizes the error decay between Q^κT\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{T} and Q^κ∗\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*} and shows that it decays exponentially in the number of Bellman iterations by a γT\gamma^{T} multiplicative factor.

B.1 Identity-Aware Sampling Algorithm and Analyses

We present an identity-aware subsampling algorithm that explicitly retains the indices of sampled neighbors within the state representation. We provide this as a simple baseline to demonstrate how subsampling and graphon-based weights can be used to construct an unbiased estimator of neighborhood-dependent rewards and transitions. The numerical stability of this approach follows the framework from Anand et al. (2024). We use this baseline to motivate the statistical guarantees of our main algorithm; specifically, we show that while identity-aware representations provide unbiasedness, their state-action space cardinality grows exponentially with κ\kappa. This motivates the mean-field reparameterization introduced in the main text.

Algorithm analysis. In Algorithm 10, the Monte Carlo samples can be derived from standard MCMC or uniform sampling methods (Chapelle and Li, 2011; Vempala and Wibisono, 2019; May et al., 2012; Munos, 2014; Riquelme et al., 2018; Anand and Liaw, 2025). The main limitation of this approach is the dimensionality of the augmented state space. The number of possible neighborhood tuples in 𝒴\mathcal{Y} scales as (|𝒮|​|𝒜|)κ(|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|)^{\kappa}. Consequently, the cardinality of the tabular identity-aware QQ-function is |𝒮|​|𝒜|⋅(|𝒮|​|𝒜|)κ=(|𝒮|​|𝒜|)κ+1|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|\cdot(|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|)^{\kappa}=(|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|)^{\kappa+1}.

The exponential dependence on the subsampling parameter κ\kappa motivates the mean-field reparameterization used throughout the GMFS model. Instead of learning on the labeled space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, we map a sampled labeled neighborhood yy to an unlabeled empirical distribution Z^iκ\hat{Z}_{i}^{\kappa}. This representation discards explicit neighbor identities but retains the aggregate information required for the reward and transition dynamics. The reparameterization thus makes learning tractable by replacing an exponentially large labeled neighborhood space with a distributional state summary whose complexity depends on |𝒮|​|𝒜||\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}| instead.

Definition B.8 (Horvitz-Thompson estimator).

Let qq be a proposal distribution on a finite set 𝒥\mathcal{J} and let ww be a target weight vector with w⁡(j)≥0w(j)\geq 0 such that ∑j∈𝒥w⁡(j)=1\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}w(j)=1, and q⁡(j)>0q(j)>0 whenever w⁡(j)>0w(j)>0. For any function ϕ:𝒥→ℝ\phi:\mathcal{J}\to\mathbb{R}, sample J1,…,Jκ∼i.i.d.qJ_{1},\dots,J_{\kappa}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}q and define the Horvitz-Thompson estimator

Φ^κ​(ϕ)≔1κ​∑m=1κw⁡(Jm)q⁡(Jm)​ϕ​(Jm).\hat{\Phi}_{\kappa}(\phi)\coloneqq\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\frac{w(J_{m})}{q(J_{m})}\phi(J_{m}). (4)

Then 𝔼⁡[Φ^κ​(ϕ)]=∑j∈𝒥w⁡(j)​ϕ​(j)\mathbb{E}[\hat{\Phi}_{\kappa}(\phi)]=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}w(j)\phi(j).

Lemma B.9 (Unbiasedness of the neighborhood estimator).

Assume qi​(j)>0q_{i}(j)>0 for all jj with w¯i​j>0\bar{w}_{ij}>0. Next, define the importance sampling weights ρ(m)\rho^{(m)} such that

ρ(m)=w¯i​J(m)qi​(J(m)).\rho^{(m)}=\frac{\bar{w}_{iJ^{(m)}}}{q_{i}(J^{(m)})}. (5)

Then the importance weighted estimator Z^i(κ)​(s,a)\hat{Z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(s,a) is an unbiased estimator of the true neighborhood aggregate Zi​(s,a)=∑j≠iw¯i​j​𝟙​{sj=s,aj=a}Z_{i}(s,a)=\sum_{j\neq i}\bar{w}_{ij}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{j}=s,a_{j}=a\} under proposal distribution qiq_{i}.

Proof.

By linearity of expectations, we have

𝔼⁡[Z^i(κ)​(s,a)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{Z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(s,a)] =𝔼⁡[1κ​∑m=1κw¯i​J(m)qi​(J(m))​𝟙​{sJi(m)=s,aJi(m)=a}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\frac{\bar{w}_{iJ^{(m)}}}{q_{i}(J^{(m)})}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{J_{i}^{(m)}}=s,a_{J_{i}^{(m)}}=a\}\Big]
=1κ​∑m=1κ𝔼⁡[w¯i​J(m)qi​(J(m))​𝟙​{sJi(m)=s,aJi(m)=a}],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\bar{w}_{iJ^{(m)}}}{q_{i}(J^{(m)})}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{J_{i}^{(m)}}=s,a_{J_{i}^{(m)}}=a\}\Big],

where

𝔼⁡[w¯i​J(m)qi​(J(m))​𝟙​{sJi(m)=s,aJi(m)=a}]=𝔼⁡[w¯i​Jqi​(J)​𝟙​{sJ=s,aJ=a}]\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\bar{w}_{iJ^{(m)}}}{q_{i}(J^{(m)})}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{J_{i}^{(m)}}=s,a_{J_{i}^{(m)}}=a\}\Big]=\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\bar{w}_{iJ}}{q_{i}(J)}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{J}=s,a_{J}=a\}\Big]

as the Ji(m)J_{i}^{(m)}’s are drawn i.i.d. Therefore,

𝔼⁡[Z^i(κ)​(s,a)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{Z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(s,a)] =𝔼⁡[w¯i​Jqi​(J)​𝟙​{sJ=s,aJ=a}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\bar{w}_{iJ}}{q_{i}(J)}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{J}=s,a_{J}=a\}\Big]
=∑j≠iqi​(j)​w¯i​jqi​(j)​𝟙​{sj=s,aj=a}\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq i}q_{i}(j)\frac{\bar{w}_{ij}}{q_{i}(j)}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{j}=s,a_{j}=a\}
=∑j≠iw¯i​j​𝟙​{sj=s,aj=a}\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq i}\bar{w}_{ij}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{j}=s,a_{j}=a\}
=Zi​(s,a),\displaystyle=Z_{i}(s,a),

where the second equality follows by using J∈[n]\{i}J\in[n]\backslash\{i\}. We conclude that since 𝔼⁡[Z^i(κ)​(s,a)]=Zi​(s,a)\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{Z}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(s,a)\big]=Z_{i}(s,a), the estimator is unbiased and thus a Horvitz-Thompson estimator.
∎

Lemma B.10 (Horvitz-Thompson unbiasedness for identity-aware neighborhoods).

Let qiq_{i} be a proposal distribution on [n]\{i}[n]\backslash\{i\}, such that qi​(j)>0q_{i}(j)>0 for all jj with w¯i​j>0\bar{w}_{ij}>0. Define the importance weights:

ρ(m)=w¯i​J(m)qi​(J(m))\rho^{(m)}=\frac{\bar{w}_{iJ^{(m)}}}{q_{i}(J^{(m)})}

Then for any function φ:([n]\{i})×𝒮×𝒜→ℝ\varphi:([n]\backslash\{i\})\times\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}, the Horvitz-Thompson estimator

Φ^i(κ)​(φ)=1κ​∑m=1κρ(m)​φ​(Ji(m),sJi(m),aJi(m))\hat{\Phi}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(\varphi)=\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\rho^{(m)}\varphi(J_{i}^{(m)},s_{J_{i}^{(m)}},a_{J_{i}^{(m)}}) (6)

is unbiased for the graphon-weighted neighborhood: Φi​(φ)=∑j≠iw¯i​j​φ​(j,sj,aj)\Phi_{i}(\varphi)=\sum_{j\neq i}\bar{w}_{ij}\varphi(j,s_{j},a_{j}), i.e. 𝔼⁡[Φ^i(κ)​(φ)]=Φi​(φ)\mathbb{E}[\hat{\Phi}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(\varphi)]=\Phi_{i}(\varphi)

Proof.

By linearity of expectation and i.i.d. sampling, we have

𝔼⁡[Φ^i(κ)​(φ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{\Phi}_{i}^{(\kappa)}(\varphi)] =𝔼⁡[w¯i​jqi​(j)​φ​(J,sJ,aJ)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\bar{w}_{ij}}{q_{i}(j)}\varphi(J,s_{J},a_{J})\Big]
=∑j≠iqi​(j)​w¯i​jqi​(j)​φ​(j,sj,aj)\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq i}q_{i}(j)\frac{\bar{w}_{ij}}{q_{i}(j)}\varphi(j,s_{j},a_{j})
=∑j≠iw¯i​j​φ​(j,sj,aj)\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq i}\bar{w}_{ij}\varphi(j,s_{j},a_{j})
=Φi​(φ)\displaystyle=\Phi_{i}(\varphi)

which proves the claim.∎

When no subsampling occurs (at κ=n−1\kappa=n-1), GMFS recovers the graphon mean-field MARL formulation corresponding to interaction graphon WW. As κ→n−1\kappa\to n-1, we show that Q^κ∗→Q∗\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}\to Q^{*} via a Lipschitz continuity bound between Q∗Q^{*} and Q^κ∗\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}.

|𝔼(s′,g′)∼𝒥n(⋅|s,a,z)maxa′,z′Qt(s′,a′,z′)−𝔼(s′,g^′)∼𝒥κ(⋅|s,a,z^)maxa′,z^′Q^κt(s′,a′,z^′)|≤4​‖rℓ‖∞1−γLP⋅TV(gz,gz^),|\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{J}_{n}(\cdot|s,a,z)}\max_{a^{\prime},z^{\prime}}Q^{t}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},z^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{(s^{\prime},\hat{g}^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}(\cdot|s,a,\hat{z})}\max_{a^{\prime},\hat{z}^{\prime}}\hat{Q}^{t}_{\kappa}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},\hat{z}^{\prime})|\leq\frac{4\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}L_{P}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(g_{z},g_{\hat{z}}),
