Definition C.7 (Joint transition probability kernel).

Fix an agent i∈[n]i\in[n]. Let ss and aa denote the state and action of agent ii and z^\hat{z} denote its graphon-weighted state/action feature on a sample of size κ\kappa (which we denote by OPENΔi)\Delta_{i}). Let the state marginals of z^\hat{z} be g^\hat{g}. The joint transition probability kernel for agent ii and its neighborhood is then:

𝒥Δi∪{i}(s′,g^′|s,a,z^).\mathcal{J}_{\Delta_{i}\cup\{i\}}(s^{\prime},\hat{g}^{\prime}|s,a,\hat{z}).
Definition C.8 (Single Agent Transition Kernel).

The single agent transition kernel for agent ii is given by the marginal

𝒥1(si′|si,sΔi,ai,aΔi)=∑sΔi′𝒥Δi∪{i}(si′,sΔi′|si,sΔi,ai,aΔi).\mathcal{J}_{1}\bigl(s_{i}^{\prime}|s_{i},s_{\Delta_{i}},a_{i},a_{\Delta_{i}}\bigr)=\sum_{s_{\Delta_{i}}^{\prime}}\mathcal{J}_{\Delta_{i}\cup\{i\}}\bigl(s_{i}^{\prime},s_{\Delta_{i}}^{\prime}|s_{i},s_{\Delta_{i}},a_{i},a_{\Delta_{i}}\bigr).
Lemma C.9.

Assuming that the next state of agent ii is conditionally independent of the neighbors’ next states given the current states and actions, the kernel 𝒥1\mathcal{J}_{1} satisfies:

ℙ⁡(Si′=si′|si,sΔi,ai,aΔi)=𝒥1​(si′|si,sΔi,ai,aΔi)\mathbb{P}\left(S_{i}^{\prime}=s_{i}^{\prime}|s_{i},s_{\Delta_{i}},a_{i},a_{\Delta_{i}}\right)=\mathcal{J}_{1}\big(s_{i}^{\prime}|s_{i},s_{\Delta_{i}},a_{i},a_{\Delta_{i}}\big)
Proof.
ℙ⁡(Si′=si′|si,sΔi,ai,aΔi)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(S_{i}^{\prime}=s_{i}^{\prime}|s_{i},s_{\Delta_{i}},a_{i},a_{\Delta_{i}}\right) =∑sΔi′ℙ(Si′=si′,SΔi=sΔi′|si,sΔi,ai,aΔi)\displaystyle=\sum_{s^{\prime}_{\Delta_{i}}}\mathbb{P}\left(S_{i}^{\prime}=s_{i}^{\prime},S_{\Delta_{i}}=s_{\Delta_{i}}^{\prime}|s_{i},s_{\Delta_{i}},a_{i},a_{\Delta_{i}}\right)
=∑sΔi′𝒥Δi∪{i}(si′,sΔi′|si,sΔi,ai,aΔi)\displaystyle=\sum_{s_{\Delta_{i}}^{\prime}}\mathcal{J}_{\Delta_{i}\cup\{i\}}\bigl(s_{i}^{\prime},s_{\Delta_{i}}^{\prime}|s_{i},s_{\Delta_{i}},a_{i},a_{\Delta_{i}}\bigr)
=𝒥1​(si′|si,sΔi,ai,aΔi),\displaystyle=\mathcal{J}_{1}\bigl(s_{i}^{\prime}|s_{i},s_{\Delta_{i}},a_{i},a_{\Delta_{i}}\bigr),

where the first equality follows by evaluating the conditional probability, and the second equality follows by definition C.8. Together, this proves the lemma.∎

We now prove a contraction property in TV-distance between the stochastic kernels 𝒥κ\mathcal{J}_{\kappa} and 𝒥\mathcal{J} under a common neighborhood.

Lemma C.10 (Coupling stability of the surrogate kernel).

Fix (s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}. Let z∈𝒫⁡(𝒮×𝒜)z\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}) and let z^∈𝒵κ\hat{z}\in\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa} be any empirical histogram; write g≔gzg\coloneqq g_{z} and g^≔gz^\hat{g}\coloneqq g_{\hat{z}}. Then, under the dynamics of 𝒥n\mathcal{J}_{n} and 𝒥κ\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}, there exists a coupling of (S0′,g′)(S^{\prime}_{0},g^{\prime}) and (S^0′,g^′)(\hat{S}^{\prime}_{0},\hat{g}^{\prime}) such that Pr[S0′≠S^0′]≤TV(P(⋅∣s,a,g),P(⋅∣s,a,g^))≤LP⋅TV(g,g^)\Pr[S^{\prime}_{0}\neq\hat{S}^{\prime}_{0}]\leq\mathrm{TV}\!\left(P(\cdot\mid s,a,g),P(\cdot\mid s,a,\hat{g})\right)\leq L_{P}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(g,\hat{g}) and

𝔼⁡[TV⁡(g′,g^′)]≤LP⋅TV⁡(g,g^).\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{TV}(g^{\prime},\hat{g}^{\prime})\big]\leq L_{P}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(g,\hat{g}).\\ (7)
Proof.

For the focal agent, take a maximal coupling of P(⋅∣s,a,g)P(\cdot\mid s,a,g) and P(⋅∣s,a,g^)P(\cdot\mid s,a,\hat{g}), so that

Pr[S0′≠S^0′]=TV(P(⋅∣s,a,g),P(⋅∣s,a,g^)).\Pr[S^{\prime}_{0}\neq\hat{S}^{\prime}_{0}]=\mathrm{TV}(P(\cdot\mid s,a,g),P(\cdot\mid s,a,\hat{g})).

Then, applying the Lipschitz continuity of the transition kernels from Assumption 3.7 completes the proof of the first inequality. For the second inequality, we consider the neighborhood marginal. Couple the two constructions by using the same i.i.d. draws (Xm,Um)∼z(X_{m},U_{m})\sim z and, conditional on each (Xm,Um)(X_{m},U_{m}), couple Xm′∼P(⋅∣Xm,Um,g)X^{\prime}_{m}\sim P(\cdot\mid X_{m},U_{m},g) with X^m′∼P(⋅∣Xm,Um,g^)\hat{X}^{\prime}_{m}\sim P(\cdot\mid X_{m},U_{m},\hat{g}) via an optimal coupling. Then, from Assumption 3.7, we have that

Pr[Xm′≠X^m′∣Xm,Um]\displaystyle\Pr[X^{\prime}_{m}\neq\hat{X}^{\prime}_{m}\mid X_{m},U_{m}] =TV(P(⋅∣Xm,Um,g),P(⋅∣Xm,Um,g^))\displaystyle=\mathrm{TV}\!\left(P(\cdot\mid X_{m},U_{m},g),P(\cdot\mid X_{m},U_{m},\hat{g})\right)
≤LP⋅TV⁡(g,g^),.\displaystyle\leq L_{P}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(g,\hat{g}),.

Next, let D≔∑m=1κ𝟙{Xm′≠X^m′}D\coloneqq\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\mathbbm{1}\{X^{\prime}_{m}\neq\hat{X}^{\prime}_{m}\} be the number of mismatches. A single mismatch can change the empirical histogram by at most 2/κ2/\kappa in ℓ1\ell_{1}, hence at most 1/κ1/\kappa in TV. Therefore, deterministically, we have

‖g′−g^′‖1≤2​Dκ⟹12​‖g′−g^′‖1≤Dκ.\displaystyle\|g^{\prime}-\hat{g}^{\prime}\|_{1}\leq\frac{2D}{{\kappa}}\implies\frac{1}{2}\|g^{\prime}-\hat{g}^{\prime}\|_{1}\leq\frac{D}{\kappa}.

Finally, taking expectations and using linearity, we have

𝔼⁡[TV⁡(g′,g^′)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{TV}(g^{\prime},\hat{g}^{\prime})] ≤1κ∑m=1κPr[Xm′≠X^m′]≤LP⋅TV(g,g^),\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\Pr[X^{\prime}_{m}\neq\hat{X}^{\prime}_{m}]\leq L_{P}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(g,\hat{g}),

which completes the proof. ∎

Lemma C.11 (Total variation contraction under mixture kernels).

Let (𝒵,𝒜)(\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{A}) be the index measurable space and (𝒳,ℬ)(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}) be the output measurable space. Let J1(⋅|z)J_{1}(\cdot|z) be a Markov kernel from 𝒵\mathcal{Z} to 𝒳\mathcal{X}. For probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, define the mixtures Jμ​(B)=∫𝒵J1​(B|z)​μ​(𝑑z)J_{\mu}(B)=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}J_{1}(B|z)\mu(\mathrm{d}z) and Jν​(B)≔∫𝒵J1​(B|z)​ν​(𝑑z)J_{\nu}(B)\coloneqq\int_{\mathcal{Z}}J_{1}(B|z)\nu(\mathrm{d}z) for all B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B}. Then,

TV⁡(𝒥μ,𝒥ν)≤TV⁡(μ,ν).\mathrm{TV}(\mathcal{J}_{\mu},\mathcal{J}_{\nu})\leq\mathrm{TV}(\mu,\nu). (8)
Proof.

Note that the lemma is a special case of the data processing inequality for ff-divergences, where f⁡(t)=12​|t−1|f(t)=\frac{1}{2}|t-1|. To prove it, we use that for probability measures P,QP,Q on a measurable space,

TV⁡(P,Q)=supB|P⁡(B)−Q⁡(B)|=12​sup‖f‖∞≤1|f​d​(P−Q)|.\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)=\sup_{B}|P(B)-Q(B)|=\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\|f\|_{\infty}\leq 1}\left|f\mathrm{d}(P-Q)\right|.

So, fix any measurable B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B} and let δ≔μ−ν\delta\coloneqq\mu-\nu be a signed measure on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, where δ⁡(𝒵)=0\delta(\mathcal{Z})=0. Then,

Jμ​(B)−Jν​(B)\displaystyle J_{\mu}(B)-J_{\nu}(B) =∫𝒵J1​(B|z)​δ​(𝑑z)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}J_{1}(B|z)\delta(\mathrm{d}z)
=12​∫(2​J1​(B|z)−1)​𝑑δ,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int(2J_{1}(B|z)-1)\mathrm{d}\delta,

where the last equality follows from ∫1​𝑑δ=δ⁡(𝒵)=0\int 1d\delta=\delta(\mathcal{Z})=0. Then, define ϕB​(z)≔2​J1​(B|z)−1\phi_{B}(z)\coloneqq 2J_{1}(B|z)-1. Since J1​(B|z)∈[0,1]J_{1}(B|z)\in[0,1], we have ϕB​(z)∈[−1,1]\phi_{B}(z)\in[-1,1] and hence ‖ϕB‖∞≤1\|\phi_{B}\|_{\infty}\leq 1.

Therefore, we write

|Jμ​(B)−Jν​(B)|\displaystyle|J_{\mu}(B)-J_{\nu}(B)| =12​|ϕB​d​(μ−ν)|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left|\phi_{B}\mathrm{d}(\mu-\nu)\right|
≤12​sup‖f‖∞≤1|f​d​(μ−ν)|\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\|f\|_{\infty}\leq 1}\left|f\mathrm{d}(\mu-\nu)\right|
=TV⁡(μ,ν).\displaystyle=\mathrm{TV}(\mu,\nu).

Since this holds for every B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B}, taking the supremum gives

TV⁡(Jμ,Jν)=supB|Jμ​(B)−Jν​(B)|≤TV⁡(μ,ν),\mathrm{TV}(J_{\mu},J_{\nu})=\sup_{B}|J_{\mu}(B)-J_{\nu}(B)|\leq\mathrm{TV}(\mu,\nu),

which proves the claim.∎

Lemma C.12 (Reward expectation mismatch under subsampling).

Let r~:𝒮×𝒢→ℝ\tilde{r}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{R} be a bounded local immediate reward with ‖rℓ‖∞<∞\|{r}_{\ell}\|_{\infty}<\infty. Let μ[n]\mu_{[n]} and μ^Δ\hat{\mu}_{\Delta} are distributions on the index space from Lemma C.11. Next, define the induced transition kernels

𝒥n(⋅)=∫𝒥1(⋅∣z)μ[n](dz)\mathcal{J}_{n}(\cdot)=\int\mathcal{J}_{1}(\cdot\mid z)\mu_{[n]}(\mathrm{d}z) (9)

and

𝒥κ(⋅)=∫𝒥1(⋅∣z)μ^Δ(dz),\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}(\cdot)=\int\mathcal{J}_{1}(\cdot\mid z)\hat{\mu}_{\Delta}(\mathrm{d}z), (10)

where 𝒥1(⋅∣z)\mathcal{J}_{1}(\cdot\mid z) is the single-agent transition kernel. The reward expectation mismatch is then given by

|𝔼𝒥n[r~(x,g′)]−𝔼𝒥κ[r~(x,g^′]|≤2∥rℓ∥∞⋅TV(μ[n],μ^Δ).|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{J}_{n}}[\tilde{r}(x,g^{\prime})]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}}[\tilde{r}(x,\hat{g}^{\prime}]|\leq 2\|{r}_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(\mu_{[n]},\hat{\mu}_{\Delta}).
Proof.

By expanding the expectations and using |r~|≤‖rℓ‖∞|\tilde{r}|\leq\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}, we have

|𝔼𝒥n[r~(x,g′)]−𝔼𝒥κ[r~(x,g^′]|\displaystyle|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{J}_{n}}[\tilde{r}(x,g^{\prime})]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}}[\tilde{r}(x,\hat{g}^{\prime}]| ≤∑(x,g′)∈𝒮×𝒢|𝒥n(x,g′|⋅)−𝒥κ(x,g′|⋅)||r~ℓ(x,g′)|\displaystyle\leq\sum_{(x,g^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{G}}\bigl|\mathcal{J}_{n}(x,g^{\prime}|\cdot)-\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}(x,g^{\prime}|\cdot)\bigr||\tilde{r}_{\ell}(x,g^{\prime})|
≤∥rℓ∥∞⋅∑(x,g′)∼𝒮×𝒢|𝒥n(x,g′|⋅)−𝒥κ(x,g′|⋅)|\displaystyle\leq\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\cdot\sum_{(x,g^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{G}}\left|\mathcal{J}_{n}(x,g^{\prime}|\cdot)-\mathcal{J}_{\kappa}(x,g^{\prime}|\cdot)\right|
=2​‖rℓ‖∞⋅TV⁡(𝒥n,𝒥κ)\displaystyle=2\|{r}_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(\mathcal{J}_{n},\mathcal{J}_{\kappa})

Now we bound the total variation distance between the two kernels. Since 𝒥n\mathcal{J}_{n} and 𝒥κ\mathcal{J}_{\kappa} are mixture kernels induced by μ[n]\mu_{[n]} and μ^Δ\hat{\mu}_{\Delta}, lemma C.11 gives TV⁡(𝒥n,𝒥κ)≤TV⁡(μ[n],μ^Δ)\mathrm{TV}(\mathcal{J}_{n},\mathcal{J}_{\kappa})\leq\mathrm{TV}(\mu_{[n]},\hat{\mu}_{\Delta}). Hence, the bound on our expectation mismatch is

|𝔼Jn[r~(x,g′)]−𝔼Jκ[r~(x,g^′]|≤2∥rℓ∥∞⋅TV(μ[n],μ^Δ),|\mathbb{E}_{J_{n}}[\tilde{r}(x,g^{\prime})]-\mathbb{E}_{J_{\kappa}}[\tilde{r}(x,\hat{g}^{\prime}]|\leq 2\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(\mu_{[n]},\hat{\mu}_{\Delta}),

which completes our proof.∎

C.1 Concentration on the Subsampled Mean-Field Features

Fix κ∈[n−1]\kappa\in[n-1]. We now wish to bound the TV-distance between the true graphon-weighted neighborhood feature gg and its subsampled estimate g^\hat{g}. Since gg is a probability mass over a finite discrete space 𝒮\mathcal{S} and g^\hat{g} is the empirical distribution formed by κ\kappa i.i.d. samples drawn from gig_{i}, we can argue a concentration bound using a similar argument as in Anand and Qu (2024).

We begin by stating the probability model.

Lemma C.13 (i.i.d. neighbor-state sampling).

Fix an agent ii and condition on the global joint state s⁡(t)=(s1​(t),…,sn​(t))s(t)=(s_{1}(t),\dots,s_{n}(t)). Define the ground-truth graphon-weighted neighborhood state distribution for x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S} by

gi(x)≔∑j≠iw¯i​j𝟙{sj(t)=x},g_{i}(x)\coloneqq\sum_{j\neq i}\bar{w}_{ij}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{j}(t)=x\},

where w¯i​j\bar{w}_{ij} are the normalized interaction weights from Definition 2.1. Then, sample neighbor indices J1(1),…,Ji(κ)∼w¯iJ_{1}^{(1)},\dots,J_{i}^{(\kappa)}\sim\bar{w}_{i} and define the sampled neighbor states Xm≔sJi(m)∈𝒮X_{m}\coloneqq s_{J_{i}^{(m)}}\in\mathcal{S}. Then, conditional on ss, the random variables X1,…,XκX_{1},\dots,X_{\kappa} are i.i.d. with law gig_{i}. In other words, Pr⁡[Xm=x|s]=gi​(x)\Pr[X_{m}=x|s]=g_{i}(x), for all x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S} and m=1,…,κm=1,\dots,\kappa.

Proof.

The proof follows by noting that

Pr⁡[Xm=x|s]\displaystyle\Pr[X_{m}=x|s] =∑j≠iPr[Ji(m)=j]𝟙{sj=x}\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq i}\Pr[J_{i}^{(m)}=j]\mathbbm{1}\{s_{j}=x\}
=∑j≠iw¯i​j𝟙{sj=x}\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq i}\bar{w}_{ij}\mathbbm{1}\{s_{j}=x\}
=gi​(x),\displaystyle=g_{i}(x),

where independence follows from the i.i.d sampling of Ji(m)J_{i}^{(m)}.∎

Theorem C.14 (TV concentration for empirical distributions on a finite alphabet).

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a finite set, and let X1,…,XκX_{1},\dots,X_{\kappa} be i.i.d. samples from a distribution p∈Δ⁡(𝒮)p\in\Delta(\mathcal{S}). Let p^\hat{p} be the empirical distribution given by p^(x)≔1κ∑m=1κ𝟙{Xm=x}\hat{p}(x)\coloneqq\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\mathbbm{1}\{X_{m}=x\}. Then, for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we have that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

TV⁡(p^,p)≤|𝒮|​ln⁡2+ln⁡(2/δ)2​κ\mathrm{TV}(\hat{p},p)\leq\sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal{S}|\ln 2+\ln(2/\delta)}{2\kappa}}

Recall that

TV⁡(p^,p)=supE⊆𝒮|p^​(E)−p⁡(E)|,\mathrm{TV}(\hat{p},p)=\sup_{E\subseteq\mathcal{S}}|\hat{p}(E)-p(E)|,

where p^​(E)≔∑x∈Ep^​(x)\hat{p}(E)\coloneqq\sum_{x\in E}\hat{p}(x). Fix any subset E⊆SE\subseteq S, and define Ym≔𝟙{Xm∈E}∈{0,1}Y_{m}\coloneqq\mathbbm{1}\{X_{m}\in E\}\in\{0,1\}. Then, Y1,…,YκY_{1},\dots,Y_{\kappa} are i.i.d. Bernoulli with mean p⁡(E)p(E) and p^​(E)=1κ​∑m=1κYm\hat{p}(E)=\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}Y_{m}.

=2|𝒮|+1​exp⁡(−2​κ​ϵ2).\displaystyle=2^{|\mathcal{S}|+1}\exp(-2\kappa\epsilon^{2}).

Finally, reparameterizing by setting δ=2|𝒮|+1​exp⁡(−2​κ​ϵ2)\delta=2^{|\mathcal{S}|+1}\exp(-2\kappa\epsilon^{2}) yields the claim.∎

D.1 Bounding the Bellman Error

To bound the Bellman error ϵk,m\epsilon_{k,m}, we first recall Hoeffding’s inequality (Hoeffding, 1963).

Lemma D.10 (Hoeffding’s inequality).

Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n} be independent random variables such that ai≤Xi≤bia_{i}\leq X_{i}\leq b_{i} almost surely. Let Sn=∑i=1nXiS_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}. Then, for all t>0t>0, we have that

Pr[|Sn−𝔼[Sn]|≥t]≤2exp(−2​t2∑i=1n(bi−ai)2).\Pr[|S_{n}-\mathbb{E}[S_{n}]|\geq t]\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{2t^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}}\right).
Lemma D.11.

Fix κ≥1\kappa\geq 1 and let 𝒯^κ\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa} and 𝒯^κ,m\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m} be as in Definitions 3.9 and 3.10. Let Q^κ∗\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*} denote the unique fixed point of 𝒯^κ\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa} and Q^κ,m∗\hat{Q}_{\kappa,m}^{*} the unique fixed point of 𝒯^κ,m\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}. Let Nκ≔|𝒮|2​|𝒜|2​κ|𝒮|​|𝒜|N_{\kappa}\coloneqq|\mathcal{S}|^{2}|\mathcal{A}|^{2}\kappa^{|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|}. Then for any ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho over the sampling used to form 𝒯^κ,m\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa,m}, we have

As in Anand et al. (2025a), this section extends the GMFS framework to environments where rewards are stochastic. Remark E.5.

From Lemma E.4, we have that in order to keep the reward-averaging contribution to be at most 1κ\frac{1}{\sqrt{\kappa}} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, it suffices to choose

Ξ≥ΔL2​κ2⋅ln⁡(2​|𝒮​‖𝒜‖​𝒢κ|δ).\Xi\geq\frac{\Delta_{L}^{2}\kappa}{2}\cdot\ln\left(\frac{2|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}|}{\delta}\right).\\ (19)

Through this averaging argument, we observe that as the subsampling parameter κ\kappa increases, the optimality gap decays to zero while the probability of success approaches one. The argument can be strengthened by estimating ℒ^\hat{\mathcal{L}} and  ^\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=6.25002pt} ℒ\textstyle\mathcal{L} using order statistics to bound estimation errors. This extension would be an essential step in transitioning this framework to a fully online learning setting via a stochastic approximation scheme. Furthermore, one could incorporate variance-based analysis (Jin et al., 2024), leveraging the skewness of the reward distribution and allowing for the assignment of optimism or pessimism scores to the resulting estimates.

Appendix F Extension to Off-Policy Learning

A limitation of the planning approach in Algorithm 1 is that it computes Q^κ∗\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*} by assuming access to a generative oracle for the transition functions Pg,PlP_{g},P_{l} and the reward function r⁡(⋅,⋅,⋅)r(\cdot,\cdot,\cdot). In certain realistic RL applications, a generative oracle like such is unavailable. Instead, it is more desirable to perform off-policy learning, where the agent learns from historical data (Fujimoto et al., 2019). In this setting, the agents learn the target policy π^κ∗\hat{\pi}_{\kappa}^{*} using a dataset generated by a different behavior policy πb\pi_{b} (the strategy used to explore the environment). There is a significant body of work on the theoretical guarantees in off-policy learning (Chen et al., 2021b; Chen and Maguluri, 2022; Chen et al., 2021c; Chen et al., 2025).

In fact, these previous results are amenable to transforming guarantees about offline QQ-learning to off-policy QQ-learning, typically at the cost of log⁡|𝒮|​|𝒜|\log|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}| factors in the sample complexity or runtime. Therefore, this section demonstrates that our previous results satisfy the necessary conditions to extend the GMFS framework to the off-policy QQ-learning for the subsampled Q^κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa}-function. We show that, in expectation, the learned policy πκ\pi_{\kappa} maintains a decaying optimality gap of O~​(1/κ)\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{\kappa}), where the randomness is over the heuristic behavior policy πb\pi_{b}.

The off-policy Q^κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa}-learning algorithm is an iterative procedure to estimate the optimal Q^κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa}-function as follows: first, a sample trajectory {(st,at,zt)}t≥0\{(s_{t},a_{t},z_{t})\}_{t\geq 0} is collected using a suitable behavior policy πb\pi_{b}. After initializing Q^κ0:𝒮×𝒜×𝒵κ→ℝ\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{0}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}\to\mathbb{R}, the iterate Q^κt​(s,a,z)\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{t}(s,a,z) is updated for each t≥0t\geq 0 according to:

Q^κt+1​(s,a,z)=(1−αt)​Q^κt​(s,a,z)+αt​(rℓ​(s,a,gz)+γ​ℳκ​Q^κt​(s′,g′)),\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{t+1}(s,a,z)=(1-\alpha_{t})\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{t}(s,a,z)+\alpha_{t}\left(r_{\ell}(s,a,g_{z})+\gamma\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{t}(s^{\prime},g^{\prime})\right), (20)

where αt∈(0,1)\alpha_{t}\in(0,1) is the learning rate. Note that the update in Equation 20 is sample-based; it does not require an expectation over the transition dynamics and can be computed directly from historical data. To ensure convergence, we make the following standard ergodicity assumption:

Assumption F.1 (Ergodicity of Behavior Policy).

The behavior policy πb\pi_{b} satisfies πb​(a|s,z)>0\pi_{b}(a|s,z)>0 for all (s,a,z)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒵κ(s,a,z)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}. Additionally, the Markov chain ℳ={(st,zt)}t≥0\mathcal{M}=\{(s_{t},z_{t})\}_{t\geq 0} induced by πb\pi_{b} is irreducible and aperiodic with stationary distribution μ\mu and mixing time: tδ​(ℳ)=min⁡{t≥0:max(s,z)∈𝒮×𝒵κ⁡‖Pt​((s,z),⋅)−μ⁡(⋅)‖TV≤δ}.t_{\delta}(\mathcal{M})=\min\left\{t\geq 0:\max_{(s,z)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{Z}_{\kappa}}\|P^{t}((s,z),\cdot)-\mu(\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq\delta\right\}. There are many heuristics for constructing such behavior policies are well-established in the literature (Fujimoto et al., 2019).

Theorem F.2.

Let πκ\pi_{\kappa} be the policy learned through off-policy Q^κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa}-learning. Under Assumption F.1, with probability at least 1−1100​eκ1-\frac{1}{100e^{\kappa}}, we have:

𝔼⁡[Vπ∗​(s0)−Vπκ​(s0)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[V^{\pi^{*}}(s_{0})-V^{\pi_{\kappa}}(s_{0})] ≤LP​‖rℓ‖∞(1−γ)2​|𝒮|​ln⁡2+|𝒜|​ln⁡20​‖rℓ‖∞​|𝒜|​κ1−γ2​κ​ln⁡40​‖rℓ‖∞​|𝒮|​|𝒜|​κ|𝒜|​|𝒮|+12(1−γ)2+2110​κ\displaystyle\leq\frac{L_{P}\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal{S}|\ln 2+|\mathcal{A}|\ln\frac{20\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}|\mathcal{A}|\kappa}{1-\gamma}}{2\kappa}}\sqrt{\ln\frac{40\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|\kappa^{|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{S}|+\frac{1}{2}}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}}+\frac{21}{10\sqrt{\kappa}}
=O~​(1/κ),\displaystyle=\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{\kappa}),

where the expectation is taken over the stochasticity of the behavior policy πb\pi_{b}.

Proposition F.3 (Analytical Properties of the Subsampled Operator).

The following properties hold for the subsampled QQ-function and the associated Markov chain:

  1. 1.

    For any s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A} and neighborhood marginals g,g′∈𝒢κg,g^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}, ‖Q^κ​(s,a,z)−Q^κ​(s,a,z′)‖≤LP1−γ​‖rℓ‖∞⋅TV⁡(g,g′)\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa}(s,a,z)-\hat{Q}_{\kappa}(s,a,z^{\prime})\|\leq\frac{L_{P}}{1-\gamma}\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}\cdot\mathrm{TV}(g,g^{\prime}) (Theorem C.3).

  2. 2.

    ‖Q^κ‖∞≤‖rℓ‖∞1−γ\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma} (Lemma B.5).

  3. 3.

    ‖𝒯^κ​Q−𝒯^κ​Q′‖∞≤γ​‖Q−Q′‖∞\|\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}Q-\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{\kappa}Q^{\prime}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma\|Q-Q^{\prime}\|_{\infty} (Lemma B.4).

  4. 4.

    The Markov chain ℳ\mathcal{M} induced by πb\pi_{b} satisfies the rapid mixing property defined in Assumption F.1.

By treating the single-trajectory update of the Q^κ\hat{Q}_{\kappa}-function as a noisy approximation of the expected update from the ideal Bellman operator, Chen et al. (2021b) uses Markovian stochastic approximation to bound the mean-squared error 𝔼⁡[‖Q^κT−Q^κ∗‖∞2]\mathbb{E}[\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{T}-\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}]. We restate their result adapted to our subsampled regime:

Theorem F.4 (Theorem 3.1 in Chen et al. (2021b) adapted to GMFS).

Suppose the learning rate is constant, αt=α\alpha_{t}=\alpha for all t≥0t\geq 0, and is chosen such that α​tα​(ℳ)≤cQ,0​(1−γ)2log⁡|𝒮|​|𝒢κ|\alpha t_{\alpha}(\mathcal{M})\leq c_{Q,0}\frac{(1-\gamma)^{2}}{\log|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}|}, where cQ,0c_{Q,0} is a numerical constant. Then, under the properties in Proposition F.3, for all t≥tα​(ℳ)t\geq t_{\alpha}(\mathcal{M}), we have:

𝔼⁡[‖Q^κt−Q^κ∗‖∞2]≤cQ,1​(1−(1−γ)​α2)t−tα​(ℳ)+cQ,2​log⁡κ|𝒮|​|𝒜|(1−γ)2​α​tα​(ℳ),\mathbb{E}[\|\hat{Q}^{t}_{\kappa}-\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}\|^{2}_{\infty}]\leq c_{Q,1}\left(1-\frac{(1-\gamma)\alpha}{2}\right)^{t-t_{\alpha}(\mathcal{M})}+c_{Q,2}\frac{\log\kappa^{|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\alpha t_{\alpha}(\mathcal{M}),

where cQ,1=3​(‖rℓ‖∞1−γ+1)2c_{Q,1}=3\left(\frac{\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}+1\right)^{2} and cQ,2=912​e​(3​‖rℓ‖∞1−γ+1)2c_{Q,2}=912e\left(\frac{3\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}+1\right)^{2}. The expectation is taken over the stochasticity of the behavior policy πb\pi_{b}.

Corollary F.5 (Corollary 3.2 in Chen et al. (2021b) adapted to our setting).

To ensure that 𝔼⁡[‖Q^κt−Q^κ∗‖∞]≤1100​κ\mathbb{E}[\|\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{t}-\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}\|_{\infty}]\leq\frac{1}{100\sqrt{\kappa}}, the required number of iterations tt satisfies:

t>O~​(κ​log2⁡(100​κ)​|𝒮|​|𝒜|​κ|𝒜|​|𝒮|(1−γ)5).t>\tilde{O}\left(\frac{\kappa\log^{2}(100\sqrt{\kappa})|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|\kappa^{|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{S}|}}{(1-\gamma)^{5}}\right).

With this sample complexity, we recover an expected value analog of Theorem 4.3 via the triangle inequality.

Corollary F.6.

For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, we have:

𝔼⁡[Q^κ∗​(s,a,z^)−Qn∗​(s,a,z)]≤LP​‖rℓ‖∞1−γ​|𝒮|​ln⁡2+ln⁡(2/δ)2​κ,\mathbb{E}[\hat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}(s,a,\hat{z})-Q_{n}^{*}(s,a,z)]\leq\frac{L_{P}\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{1-\gamma}\sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal{S}|\ln 2+\ln(2/\delta)}{2\kappa}},

where the expectation is taken over the stochasticity of the behavior policy πb\pi_{b}.

In turn, following the derivation in the proof of Theorem 4.3, it is straightforward to verify that this yields a bound on the expected performance difference for off-policy learning.

Corollary F.7.

With probability at least 1−1100​eκ1-\frac{1}{100e^{\kappa}}, the expected performance gap satisfies:

𝔼⁡[Vπ∗​(s,g)−Vπκ​(s,g)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[V^{\pi^{*}}(s,g)-V^{\pi_{\kappa}}(s,g)] ≤LP​‖rℓ‖∞(1−γ)2​|𝒮|​ln⁡2+|𝒜|​ln⁡20​‖rℓ‖∞​|𝒜|​κ1−γ2​κ​ln⁡40​‖rℓ‖∞​|𝒮|​|𝒜|​κ|𝒜|​|𝒮|+12(1−γ)2+2110​κ\displaystyle\leq\frac{L_{P}\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal{S}|\ln 2+|\mathcal{A}|\ln\frac{20\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}|\mathcal{A}|\kappa}{1-\gamma}}{2\kappa}}\sqrt{\ln\frac{40\|r_{\ell}\|_{\infty}|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|\kappa^{|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{S}|+\frac{1}{2}}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}}+\frac{21}{10\sqrt{\kappa}}

where the expectation is taken over the stochasticity of the behavior policy πb\pi_{b}.

Appendix G Extension to Continuous State Spaces

Multi-agent settings in which agents operate in continuous state space have numerous applications in optimization, control, and synchronization (Preiss et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023b; Lin et al., 2024). Therefore, this section is devoted to extending the tabular analysis of Section 4 to non-tabular environments with a compact (and possibly continuous) state space. The main technical differences from the finite setting are that the state space 𝒮\mathcal{S} is uncountable, hence one must work in function spaces, and the κ\kappa-sampled mean-field state space 𝒢κ\mathcal{G}_{\kappa} is infinite when 𝒮\mathcal{S} is continuous, which requires all the union bounds over |𝒢κ||\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}| (for instance, in Lemma D.8) to be replaced with covering-number arguments. For this section, we keep the mean-field as part of the state. Concretely, the representative agent’s state is x=(s,g)x=(s,g) where s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} is the agent’s local state and gg is a mean-field (neighborhood) distribution over 𝒮\mathcal{S}, which can exist over 𝒢\mathcal{G} or 𝒢κ\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}.

Definition G.1 (Augmented mean-field state space).

Let (𝒮,d𝒮)(\mathcal{S},d_{\mathcal{S}}) be a compact metric space with Borel σ\sigma-algebra ℬ⁡(𝒮)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S}). Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a finite action set (the extension to compact 𝒜\mathcal{A} is analogous via an additional action-space covering). Let ℳ≔𝒫⁡(𝒮)\mathcal{M}\coloneqq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}) be the set of Borel probability measures on 𝒮\mathcal{S}. For κ∈ℕ\kappa\in\mathbb{N}, define the κ\kappa-empirical mean-field class

ℳκ≔{1κ∑m=1κδxm:x1,…,xκ∈𝒮}⊂ℳ,\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}\coloneqq\Bigl\{\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\delta_{x_{m}}:x_{1},\dots,x_{\kappa}\in\mathcal{S}\Bigr\}\subset\mathcal{M},

which is uncountable whenever 𝒮\mathcal{S} is infinite. We define the augmented (mean-field) state spaces 𝒳≔𝒮×ℳ\mathcal{X}\coloneqq\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{M} and 𝒳κ≔𝒮×ℳκ\mathcal{X}_{\kappa}\coloneqq\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}, equipped with the product Borel σ\sigma-algebras. Then, a Markov policy is a measurable map π:𝒳→Δ⁡(𝒜)\pi:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A}).

Definition G.2 (κ\kappa-surrogate MDP).

Fix a discount γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). We consider an augmented MDP on 𝒳\mathcal{X} with reward r:𝒳×𝒜→ℝr:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} and transition kernel P¯\bar{P} from 𝒳×𝒜\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A} to 𝒳\mathcal{X}. In GMFS, P¯\bar{P} is the one-step kernel of (s,g)(s,g) under the mean-field dynamics. Likewise, define the κ\kappa-surrogate MDP on 𝒳κ\mathcal{X}_{\kappa} with reward rκr_{\kappa} and kernel P¯κ\bar{P}_{\kappa}, where P¯κ\bar{P}_{\kappa} is the distributional one-step kernel induced by the (κ+1)(\kappa+1)-agent surrogate construction that outputs (s′,g′)(s^{\prime},g^{\prime}) where s′s^{\prime} is the focal agent’s next state and g′g^{\prime} is the empirical mean-field of κ\kappa sampled neighbors.

Definition G.3 (Bellman operator on 𝒳\mathcal{X}).

For any bounded measurable Q:𝒳×𝒜×𝒵→ℝQ:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}, define the optimal Bellman operator on 𝒳\mathcal{X} by:

𝒯​V​(x)≔maxa∈𝒜⁡{rℓ​(x,a)+γ​∫𝒳V⁡(x′)​P¯​(d​x′∣x,a)}.\mathcal{T}V(x)\coloneqq\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left\{r_{\ell}(x,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}V(x^{\prime})\bar{P}(dx^{\prime}\mid x,a)\right\}. (21)

Similarly define 𝒯κ\mathcal{T}_{\kappa} on bounded V:𝒳κ→ℝV:\mathcal{X}_{\kappa}\to\mathbb{R} by replacing (r,P¯)(r,\bar{P}) with (rκ,P¯κ)(r_{\kappa},\bar{P}_{\kappa}).

Lemma G.4.

𝒯\mathcal{T} is a γ\gamma-contraction in the sup-norm, and therefore has a fixed point V∗V^{*}.

Proof.

Consider V1,V2:𝒳→ℝV_{1},V_{2}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}. Then, we have that

|𝒯​V1−𝒯​V2|\displaystyle|\mathcal{T}V_{1}-\mathcal{T}V_{2}| =|maxa∈𝒜⁡{rℓ​(x,a)+γ​∫𝒳V1​(x′)​P¯​(d​x′|x,a)}−maxa∈𝒜⁡{rℓ​(x,a)+γ​∫𝒳V2​(x′)​P¯​(d​x′|x,a)}|\displaystyle=\left|\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left\{r_{\ell}(x,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}V_{1}(x^{\prime})\bar{P}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}|x,a)\right\}-\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left\{r_{\ell}(x,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}V_{2}(x^{\prime})\bar{P}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}|x,a)\right\}\right|
≤γ⋅maxa∈𝒜⁡|∫𝒳V1​(x′)​P​(d​x′|x,a)−∫𝒳V2​(x′)​P​(d​x′|x,a)|\displaystyle\leq\gamma\cdot\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left|\int_{\mathcal{X}}V_{1}(x^{\prime})P(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}|x,a)-\int_{\mathcal{X}}V_{2}(x^{\prime})P(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}|x,a)\right|
≤γ⋅‖V1−V2‖∞,\displaystyle\leq\gamma\cdot\|V_{1}-V_{2}\|_{\infty},

where the first inequality follows by the 11-Lipschitzness of the max operator. ∎

We now impose a linear MDP structure on the augmented state spaces 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒳κ\mathcal{X}_{\kappa}).

Definition G.5 (Linear mean-field MDP on 𝒳\mathcal{X}).

The augmented MDP (𝒳,𝒜,P¯,r,γ)(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{A},\bar{P},r,\gamma) is linear of dimension dd if there exists a measurable feature map φ:𝒳×𝒜→ℝd\varphi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, a vector θ∈ℝd\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and a collection of dd signed measures μ=(μ1,…,μd)\mu=(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}) on (𝒳,ℬ⁡(𝒳))(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{X})) such that for all (x,a)∈𝒳×𝒜(x,a)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A} and all measurable B⊆𝒳B\subseteq\mathcal{X}, we have r⁡(x,a)=⟨φ⁡(x,a),θ⟩r(x,a)=\langle\varphi(x,a),\theta\rangle and P¯​(B∣x,a)=⟨φ⁡(x,a),μ⁡(B)⟩\bar{P}(B\mid x,a)=\langle\varphi(x,a),\mu(B)\rangle, where μ⁡(B)≔(μ1​(B),…,μd​(B))∈ℝd\mu(B)\coloneqq(\mu_{1}(B),\dots,\mu_{d}(B))\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Assumption G.6 (Bounded features and parameters).

Recalling Assumption 4.5, we assume WLOG that ‖φ⁡(x,a)‖2≤1\|\varphi(x,a)\|_{2}\leq 1 for all (x,a)(x,a), ‖θ‖2≤Θ\|\theta\|_{2}\leq\Theta, and ‖μ⁡(𝒳)‖2≤𝖬\|\mu(\mathcal{X})\|_{2}\leq\mathsf{M} for some finite constants Θ\Theta and 𝖬\mathsf{M}.

Assumption G.7 (Positivity/normalization).

To enforce regularity on the probability kernel φ\varphi, we assume that for all measurable BB, ⟨φ⁡(x,a),μ⁡(𝒳)⟩=1\langle\varphi(x,a),\mu(\mathcal{X})\rangle=1 and ⟨φ⁡(x,a),μ⁡(B)⟩≥0\langle\varphi(x,a),\mu(B)\rangle\geq 0.

The above assumptions imply that QπQ^{\pi} is linear in VπV^{\pi}.

Lemma G.8 (Linearity of QπQ^{\pi} in the augmented linear MDP).

Fix γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), and let (𝒳,𝒜,P,r)(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{A},P,r) be the augmented discounted MDP where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is finite. Then for any stationary policy π\pi, there exists wπ∈ℝdw^{\pi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that for all (x,a)∈𝒳×𝒜(x,a)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A},

Qπ​(x,a)=⟨φ⁡(x,a),wπ⟩.\displaystyle Q^{\pi}(x,a)=\langle\varphi(x,a),w^{\pi}\rangle. (22)

Moreover, we define the d×dd\times d matrix AπA_{\pi} where (Aπ)i​j≔∫𝒳μi​(𝑑x)​φ¯π,j​(x)(A_{\pi})_{ij}\coloneqq\int_{\mathcal{X}}\mu_{i}(\mathrm{d}x)\bar{\varphi}_{\pi,j}(x). If ‖θ‖2≤Θ,‖Aπ‖2≤1\|\theta\|_{2}\leq\Theta,\|A_{\pi}\|_{2}\leq 1 and ‖φ⁡(x,a)‖2≤1\|\varphi(x,a)\|_{2}\leq 1 for all (x,a)(x,a), then ‖wπ‖2≤Θ1−γ\|w^{\pi}\|_{2}\leq\frac{\Theta}{1-\gamma}.

𝒯π​Q​(x,a)≔r⁡(x,a)+γ​∫𝒳∑a′∈𝒜π⁡(a′∣x′)​Q​(x′,a′)​P​(d​x′∣x,a),\mathcal{T}^{\pi}Q(x,a)\coloneqq r(x,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a^{\prime}\mid x^{\prime})Q(x^{\prime},a^{\prime})P(dx^{\prime}\mid x,a), (23)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a contractive operator with module γ\gamma.

For any w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define the linear function Qw​(x,a)≔⟨φ⁡(x,a),w⟩Q_{w}(x,a)\coloneqq\langle\varphi(x,a),w\rangle and let φ¯π​(x)≔∑a∈𝒜π⁡(a∣x)​φ​(x,a)∈ℝd\bar{\varphi}_{\pi}(x)\coloneqq\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\mid x)\varphi(x,a)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the policy-averaged feature map. Hence, using submultiplicativity and ‖Aπ‖2≤1\|A_{\pi}\|_{2}\leq 1, we have

‖w(t)‖2\displaystyle\|w^{(t)}\|_{2} ≤∑h=0t−1γh​‖Aπ‖2h​‖θ‖2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{h=0}^{t-1}\gamma^{h}\|A_{\pi}\|_{2}^{h}\|\theta\|_{2}
≤‖θ‖2​∑h=0t−1γh\displaystyle\leq\|\theta\|_{2}\sum_{h=0}^{t-1}\gamma^{h}
≤‖θ‖21−γ≤Θ1−γ,\displaystyle\leq\frac{\|\theta\|_{2}}{1-\gamma}\leq\frac{\Theta}{1-\gamma},

proving the lemma.∎

We now address the function-space policy evaluation and define the projected Bellman equation.

Definition G.9 (Projected Bellman equation).

Fix a policy π\pi, and let ν\nu be any reference distribution on 𝒳∈L2​(ν)\mathcal{X}\in L_{2}(\nu), where L2​(ν)L_{2}(\nu) is the Hilbert space equipped with inner product

⟨f,h⟩L2​(ν)=∫f⁡(x)​h​(x)​ν​(𝑑x).\langle f,h\rangle_{L_{2}(\nu)}=\int f(x)h(x)\nu(dx). (25)

Then, letting φ¯π(x)≔𝔼a∼π(⋅∣x)[φ(x,a)]\bar{\varphi}_{\pi}(x)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}[\varphi(x,a)], we define the feature operator Φ:L2​(ν)←ℝd\Phi:L_{2}(\nu)\leftarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} by (Φ​w)​(x)≔⟨φ¯π​(x),w⟩(\Phi w)(x)\coloneqq\langle\bar{\varphi}_{\pi}(x),w\rangle. Let Πν\Pi_{\nu} denote the orthogonal projection in L2​(ν)L_{2}(\nu) onto range⁡(Φ)\mathrm{range}(\Phi). Then, the projected Bellman equation is given by

Φ​w≔Πν​𝒯π​(Φ​w),\displaystyle\Phi w\coloneqq\Pi_{\nu}\mathcal{T}^{\pi}(\Phi w), (26)

where

𝒯πV(x)≔𝔼a∼π(⋅∣x)[r(x,a)+γ∫V(x′)P¯(dx′∣x,a)].\displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{\pi}V(x)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}\left[r(x,a)+\gamma\int V(x^{\prime})\bar{P}(dx^{\prime}\mid x,a)\right]. (27)
Remark G.10.

Taking first-order optimality conditions yields the normal equations

𝔼x∼ν​[φ¯π​(x)​φ¯π​(x)⊤]​w=𝔼x∼ν​[φ¯π​(x)​(rπ​(x)+γ​𝔼​[Vw​(x′)∣x])],\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu}\!\Big[\bar{\varphi}_{\pi}(x)\bar{\varphi}_{\pi}(x)^{\top}\Big]w=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu}\!\Big[\bar{\varphi}_{\pi}(x)\big(r_{\pi}(x)+\gamma\mathbb{E}[V_{w}(x^{\prime})\mid x]\big)\Big],

with rπ​(x)≔𝔼a∼π​[r⁡(x,a)]r_{\pi}(x)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}[r(x,a)] and Vw​(x)≔⟨φ¯π​(x),w⟩V_{w}(x)\coloneqq\langle\bar{\varphi}_{\pi}(x),w\rangle.

We now show how to handle ℳκ\mathcal{M}_{\kappa} being uncountable by using covering numbers instead of |𝒢κ||\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}|. Specifically, in the tabular setting, we could union-bound over (s,g)∈𝒮×𝒢κ(s,g)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{G}_{\kappa} because 𝒢κ\mathcal{G}_{\kappa} was finite. However, in this setting where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is continuous, ℳκ\mathcal{M}_{\kappa} is uncountable. Therefore, we instead use a covering-number (metric-entropy) bound. For any subset 𝒱\mathcal{V} of a metric space (𝖵,d)(\mathsf{V},d), let N⁡(ε,𝒱,d)N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{V},d) denote the minimum size of an ε\varepsilon-net (Anand et al., 2025b). We observe that, under a linear MDP, all concentration arguments needed for policy evaluation/control can be reduced to controlling random quantities indexed by the feature vectors φ⁡(x,a)\varphi(x,a), not by (x,a)(x,a) directly.

Remark G.11.

Consider the feature image

𝒱κ≔{φ(x,a):x∈𝒳κ,a∈𝒜}⊆ℝd.\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\kappa}\coloneqq\{\varphi(x,a):x\in\mathcal{X}_{\kappa},a\in\mathcal{A}\}\ \subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}. (28)

By Assumption G.6, we have that 𝒱κ\mathcal{V}_{\kappa} is contained in the unit Euclidean ball 𝔹2d\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}. Specifically, for every ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1], we have

N(ε,𝒱κ,∥⋅∥2)\displaystyle N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{V}_{\kappa},\|\cdot\|_{2}) ≤N(ε,𝔹2d,∥⋅∥2)≤(3ε)d.\displaystyle\leq N(\varepsilon,\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d},\|\cdot\|_{2})\leq\Big(\frac{3}{\varepsilon}\Big)^{d}. (29)

Therefore, we can now replace any argument that previously union-bounded over |𝒮|​|𝒢κ||\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{G}_{\kappa}| by a union bound over an ε\varepsilon-net of 𝒱κ\mathcal{V}_{\kappa} with complexity d​log⁡(3/ε)d\log(3/\varepsilon).

We are now ready to state our result which decomposes the subsampling error and estimation error which arises from learning/using features in a non-tabular space.

First, in the linear-MDP setting, it suffices to control the induced error in feature expectations. We assume that the only way the mean-field enters the dynamics is through the dd-dimensional feature vector.

Assumption G.12.

There exists a bounded map ψ:𝒮×𝒜×𝒢→ℝd\psi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥ψ(s,a,⋅)∥2≤1\|\psi(s,a,\cdot)\|_{2}\leq 1 such that for all x=(s,g)∈𝒳x=(s,g)\in\mathcal{X} and a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A},

φ⁡(x,a)=∫𝒮ψ⁡(s,a,u)​g​(𝑑u).\displaystyle\varphi(x,a)=\int_{\mathcal{S}}\psi(s,a,u)g(du). (30)

As a result, if g^=1κ​∑m=1κδUm\hat{g}=\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\delta_{U_{m}} with Um∼i.i.d.gU_{m}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}g, then φ⁡((s,g^),a)=1κ​∑m=1κψ⁡(s,a,Um)\varphi((s,\hat{g}),a)=\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa}\psi(s,a,U_{m}).

Remark G.13.

Under Assumption G.12, the vector Hoeffding bound yields ‖φ⁡((s,g^),a)−φ⁡((s,g),a)‖2=O⁡(d/κ)\|\varphi((s,\hat{g}),a)-\varphi((s,g),a)\|_{2}=O\big(\sqrt{d/\kappa}\big).

Next, let φ^\widehat{\varphi} be a learned feature map (e.g. from a spectral factorization procedure). We quantify its error by

εrep≔sup(x,a)∈𝒳×𝒜‖φ^​(x,a)−φ⁡(x,a)‖2.\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rep}}\coloneqq\sup_{(x,a)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}}\|\widehat{\varphi}(x,a)-\varphi(x,a)\|_{2}. (31)

Let Q^κ\widehat{Q}_{\kappa} be the value function returned by any consistent linear evaluation/planning procedure using MM samples from a generative model on the κ\kappa-surrogate MDP, producing a greedy policy π^κ\widehat{\pi}_{\kappa}.

Theorem G.14 (Continuous-state extension with covering numbers).

Let π^κ\widehat{\pi}_{\kappa} be a greedy policy computed on the κ\kappa-surrogate using learned features φ^\widehat{\varphi} with representation error εrep≔supx,a‖φ^κ​(x,a)−φκ​(x,a)‖2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rep}}\coloneqq\sup_{x,a}\|\widehat{\varphi}_{\kappa}(x,a)-\varphi_{\kappa}(x,a)\|_{2} and MM samples. Then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), we have that with probability at least 1−3​δ1-3\delta,

supx∈𝒳[V∗​(x)−Vπ^κ​(x)]≤O~​(1(1−γ)3​d+|𝒜|+log⁡(1/δ)κ+1(1−γ)2​d​log⁡(N⁡(ε)δ)M+ε(1−γ)2+εrep(1−γ)2),\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\left[V^{*}(x)-V^{\widehat{\pi}_{\kappa}}(x)\right]\leq\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^{3}}\sqrt{\frac{d+|\mathcal{A}|+\log(1/\delta)}{\kappa}}+\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{{d\log\!\big(\frac{N(\varepsilon)}{\delta}\big)}}{{M}}}+\frac{\varepsilon}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}+\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rep}}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\right),

where 𝒱κ={φ(x,a):x∈𝒳κ,a∈𝒜}\mathcal{V}_{\kappa}=\{\varphi(x,a):x\in\mathcal{X}_{\kappa},a\in\mathcal{A}\} and N⁡(⋅)N(\cdot) is the covering number. Moreover, since 𝒱κ⊆𝔹2d\mathcal{V}_{\kappa}\subseteq\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}, we can upper bound the entropy term via (29) as logN(ε,𝒱κ,∥⋅∥2)≤dlog(3/ε)\log N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{V}_{\kappa},\|\cdot\|_{2})\ \leq\ d\log(3/\varepsilon), so the statistical term is at most O~​(d/M)\tilde{O}(d/\sqrt{M}).

Proof.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} and 𝒯~\widetilde{\mathcal{T}} be γ\gamma-contractions on (ℬ(𝒳×𝒜),∥⋅∥∞)(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}),\|\cdot\|_{\infty}) with unique fixed points Q∗Q^{*} and Q~∗\widetilde{Q}^{*}. Then,

‖Q∗−Q~∗‖∞\displaystyle\|Q^{*}-\widetilde{Q}^{*}\|_{\infty} =‖𝒯​Q∗−𝒯~​Q~∗‖∞\displaystyle=\|\mathcal{T}Q^{*}-\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{Q}^{*}\|_{\infty}
≤‖𝒯​Q∗−𝒯~​Q∗‖∞+‖𝒯~​Q∗−𝒯~​Q~∗‖∞\displaystyle\leq\|\mathcal{T}Q^{*}-\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}Q^{*}\|_{\infty}+\|\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}Q^{*}-\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{Q}^{*}\|_{\infty}
≤‖(𝒯−𝒯~)​Q∗‖∞+γ​‖Q∗−Q~∗‖∞.\displaystyle\leq\|(\mathcal{T}-\widetilde{\mathcal{T}})Q^{*}\|_{\infty}+\gamma\|Q^{*}-\widetilde{Q}^{*}\|_{\infty}.

Let Q^\widehat{Q} be any bounded function and let π^\widehat{\pi} be greedy with respect to Q^\widehat{Q}, i.e. π^(⋅∣x)∈argmaxa∈𝒜Q^(x,a)\widehat{\pi}(\cdot\mid x)\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\widehat{Q}(x,a). Then, for the true MDP,

supx∈𝒳(V∗​(x)−Vπ^​(x))≤21−γ​‖Q^−Q∗‖∞.\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\bigl(V^{*}(x)-V^{\widehat{\pi}}(x)\bigr)\leq\frac{2}{1-\gamma}\|\widehat{Q}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}. (32)

We will apply (32) with Q^=Q^κ∗\widehat{Q}=\widehat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}. Then, by the triangle inequality, ‖Q^κ∗−Q∗‖∞≤‖Qκ∗−Q∗‖∞+‖Q^κ∗−Qκ∗‖∞\|\widehat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq{\|Q_{\kappa}^{*}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}}+\|\widehat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}-Q_{\kappa}^{*}\|_{\infty}. We bound each term separately. We first bound the subsampling bias ‖Qκ∗−Q∗‖∞\|Q_{\kappa}^{*}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty} by using ‖Qκ∗−Q∗‖∞≤11−γ​‖(𝒯κ−𝒯)​Q∗‖∞\|Q_{\kappa}^{*}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\|(\mathcal{T}_{\kappa}-\mathcal{T})Q^{*}\|_{\infty}. Fix (x,a)(x,a) and let f∗​(x′)≔maxa′⁡Q∗​(x′,a′)f^{*}(x^{\prime})\coloneqq\max_{a^{\prime}}Q^{*}(x^{\prime},a^{\prime}). Then,

(𝒯κ−𝒯)​Q∗​(x,a)\displaystyle(\mathcal{T}_{\kappa}-\mathcal{T})Q^{*}(x,a) =⟨φκ​(x,a)−φ⁡(x,a),θ⟩+γ⁡⟨φκ​(x,a)−φ⁡(x,a),∫𝒳f∗​(x′)​μ​(d​x′)⟩\displaystyle=\langle\varphi_{\kappa}(x,a)-\varphi(x,a),\theta\rangle+\gamma\Big\langle\varphi_{\kappa}(x,a)-\varphi(x,a),\int_{\mathcal{X}}f^{*}(x^{\prime})\mu(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})\Big\rangle
=⟨φκ​(x,a)−φ⁡(x,a),θ+γ​∫𝒳f∗​(x′)​μ​(d​x′)⟩\displaystyle=\Big\langle\varphi_{\kappa}(x,a)-\varphi(x,a),\ \theta+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{X}}f^{*}(x^{\prime})\mu(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})\Big\rangle
≤‖φκ​(x,a)−φ⁡(x,a)‖2⋅‖θ+γ​∫f∗​𝑑μ‖2,\displaystyle\leq\|\varphi_{\kappa}(x,a)-\varphi(x,a)\|_{2}\cdot\left\|\theta+\gamma\int f^{*}\mathrm{d}\mu\right\|_{2},

where the last inequality uses Cauchy-Schwarz. We then bound the second factor using our boundedness assumption while using ‖f∗‖∞≤‖Q∗‖∞≤11−γ\|f^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\|Q^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{1-\gamma}. Specifically, for each coordinate, we have

|∫f∗​d​μi|≤‖μi‖TV​‖f∗‖∞⟹‖∫f∗​𝑑μ‖2≤‖μ‖TV,2​‖f∗‖∞≤11−γ,\displaystyle\left|\int f^{*}\mathrm{d}\mu_{i}\right|\leq\|\mu_{i}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\|f^{*}\|_{\infty}\implies\left\|\int f^{*}d\mu\right\|_{2}\leq\|\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV},2}\|f^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{1-\gamma}, (33)

Therefore, we have

‖θ+γ​∫f∗​𝑑μ‖2\displaystyle\left\|\theta+\gamma\int f^{*}d\mu\right\|_{2} ≤‖θ‖2+γ​‖∫f∗​𝑑μ‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\theta\|_{2}+\gamma\left\|\int f^{*}d\mu\right\|_{2}
≤1+γ1−γ=11−γ.\displaystyle\leq 1+\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}.

Note that by Lemma G.16, there exists a construction of φκ\varphi_{\kappa} from κ\kappa i.i.d. samples such that for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

Δκ≔sup(x,a)∈𝒳×𝒜‖φκ​(x,a)−φ⁡(x,a)‖2≤C1​d+|𝒜|+log⁡(1/δ)κ,\Delta_{\kappa}\coloneqq\sup_{(x,a)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}}\|\varphi_{\kappa}(x,a)-\varphi(x,a)\|_{2}\ \leq\ C_{1}\sqrt{\frac{d+|\mathcal{A}|+\log(1/\delta)}{\kappa}}, (34)

for a universal constant C1C_{1} . So, taking the supremum over (x,a)(x,a) yields ‖(𝒯κ−𝒯)​Q∗‖∞≤Δκ1−γ\|(\mathcal{T}_{\kappa}-\mathcal{T})Q^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\Delta_{\kappa}}{1-\gamma}. Hence, we have that

‖Qκ∗−Q∗‖∞≤Δκ(1−γ)2≤C1(1−γ)2​d+|𝒜|+log⁡(1/δ)κ.\|Q_{\kappa}^{*}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\Delta_{\kappa}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\leq\frac{C_{1}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{d+|\mathcal{A}|+\log(1/\delta)}{\kappa}}.

‖Q^κ,M∗−Qκ∗‖∞≤C21−γ⋅d​log⁡(N⁡(ε)δ)M+C21−γ⋅ε.\|\widehat{Q}_{\kappa,M}^{*}-Q_{\kappa}^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{C_{2}}{1-\gamma}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{{d\log\!\big(\frac{N(\varepsilon)}{\delta}\big)}}{{M}}}\ +\ \frac{C_{2}}{1-\gamma}\cdot\varepsilon. (35)

Finally, the representation error contributes at most C31−γ​εrep\frac{C_{3}}{1-\gamma}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rep}} (additively) to ‖Q^κ∗−Qκ∗‖∞\|\widehat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}-Q_{\kappa}^{*}\|_{\infty}. Therefore, together, we have that with probability at least 1−3​δ1-3\delta,

‖Q^κ∗−Q∗‖∞≤C1(1−γ)2​d+|𝒜|+log⁡(1/δ)κ+C21−γ⋅d​log⁡(N⁡(ε)δ)M+C21−γ⋅ε+C31−γ​εrep.\|\widehat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{C_{1}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{d+|\mathcal{A}|+\log(1/\delta)}{\kappa}}+\frac{C_{2}}{1-\gamma}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{{d\log\!\big(\frac{N(\varepsilon)}{\delta}\big)}}{{M}}}+\frac{C_{2}}{1-\gamma}\cdot\varepsilon+\frac{C_{3}}{1-\gamma}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rep}}.

Then, using supx(V∗​(x)−Vπ^κ​(x))≤21−γ​‖Q^κ∗−Q∗‖∞\sup_{x}(V^{*}(x)-V^{\widehat{\pi}_{\kappa}}(x))\leq\frac{2}{1-\gamma}\|\widehat{Q}_{\kappa}^{*}-Q^{*}\|_{\infty} proves the theorem.∎

Finally, we show how to produce a uniform concentration over 𝒱κ\mathcal{V}_{\kappa} via covering numbers.

Lemma G.15.

Let 𝒱⊆ℝd\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be any set with supv∈𝒱‖v‖2≤1\sup_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\|v\|_{2}\leq 1. Let Z1,…,ZMZ_{1},\dots,Z_{M} be i.i.d. random vectors in [−1,1]d[-1,1]^{d} with mean 𝔼⁡[Z1]=0\mathbb{E}[Z_{1}]=0. Define Z¯≔1M​∑m=1MZm\overline{Z}\coloneqq\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}Z_{m}. Fix ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1] and let N(ε)≔N(ε,𝒱,∥⋅∥2)N(\varepsilon)\coloneqq N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{V},\|\cdot\|_{2}). Then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, we have that

supv∈𝒱|⟨v,Z¯⟩|≤2​d​log⁡(2​N​(ε)δ)M+2​ε​d.\sup_{v\in\mathcal{V}}|\langle v,\overline{Z}\rangle|\ \leq\ \sqrt{\frac{2d\log\!\big(\frac{2N(\varepsilon)}{\delta}\big)}{M}}+2\varepsilon\sqrt{d}.
Proof.

Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be an ε\varepsilon-net of 𝒱\mathcal{V} in ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} of size |𝒩|=N⁡(ε)|\mathcal{N}|=N(\varepsilon). For any fixed u∈𝒩u\in\mathcal{N}, define the scalar random variables Ym​(u)≔⟨u,Zm⟩Y_{m}(u)\coloneqq\langle u,Z_{m}\rangle. Since Zm∈[−1,1]dZ_{m}\in[-1,1]^{d} and ‖u‖2≤1\|u\|_{2}\leq 1, we have

‖u‖1≤d​‖u‖2≤d⟹|Ym​(u)|≤‖u‖1≤d\|u\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{d}\|u\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\implies|Y_{m}(u)|\leq\|u\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{d}

almost surely. By Hoeffding’s inequality, we have

Pr[|⟨u,Z¯⟩|≥t]\displaystyle\Pr\left[|\langle u,\overline{Z}\rangle|\geq t\right] =Pr⁡(|1M​∑m=1MYm​(u)|≥t)\displaystyle=\Pr\Big(\Big|\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}Y_{m}(u)\Big|\geq t\Big)
≤2​exp⁡(−2​M​t2(2​d)2)=2​exp⁡(−M​t22​d).\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\Big(-\frac{2Mt^{2}}{(2\sqrt{d})^{2}}\Big)=2\exp\Big(-\frac{Mt^{2}}{2d}\Big).

Union-bounding over all u∈𝒩u\in\mathcal{N} gives Pr[supu∈𝒩|⟨u,Z¯⟩|≥t]≤2N(ε)exp(−M​t22​d)\Pr\left[\sup_{u\in\mathcal{N}}|\langle u,\overline{Z}\rangle|\geq t\right]\leq 2N(\varepsilon)\exp(-\frac{Mt^{2}}{2d}). Then, setting the right-hand side to δ\delta yields that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

supu∈𝒩|⟨u,Z¯⟩|≤2​d​log⁡(2​N​(ε)δ)M.\sup_{u\in\mathcal{N}}|\langle u,\overline{Z}\rangle|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2d\log(\frac{2N(\varepsilon)}{\delta})}{M}}.

We now extend from the net to all v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}. For any v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}, choose u∈𝒩u\in\mathcal{N} with ‖v−u‖2≤ε\|v-u\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon. Then

|⟨v,Z¯⟩|\displaystyle|\langle v,\overline{Z}\rangle| ≤|⟨u,Z¯⟩|+|⟨v−u,Z¯⟩|\displaystyle\leq|\langle u,\overline{Z}\rangle|+|\langle v-u,\overline{Z}\rangle|
≤supu∈𝒩|⟨u,Z¯⟩|+‖v−u‖2​‖Z¯‖2.\displaystyle\leq\sup_{u\in\mathcal{N}}|\langle u,\overline{Z}\rangle|+\|v-u\|_{2}\|\overline{Z}\|_{2}.

Since each coordinate of Z¯\overline{Z} lies in [−1,1][-1,1], we have that ‖Z¯‖2≤d\|\overline{Z}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}; hence, |⟨v−u,Z¯⟩|≤ε​d|\langle v-u,\overline{Z}\rangle|\leq\varepsilon\sqrt{d}. Applying the same argument to −Z¯-\overline{Z} yields the factor 2​ε​d2\varepsilon\sqrt{d} in the symmetric bound, which completes the proof.∎

Lemma G.16 (Construction of φκ\varphi_{\kappa} and a κ−1/2\kappa^{-1/2} perturbation bound).

Let p≔d+|𝒜|p\coloneqq d+|\mathcal{A}|, and consider the measurable mean-field embedding map ψ:Ξ→ℝp\psi:\Xi\to\mathbb{R}^{p} such that ‖ψ⁡(ξ)‖2≤1\|\psi(\xi)\|_{2}\leq 1 for all ξ∈Ξ\xi\in\Xi. Then, consider the population mean-field feature as u⁡(m)≔𝔼ξ∼m​[ψ⁡(ξ)]∈ℝpu(m)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim m}\big[\psi(\xi)\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, such that φ⁡((s,m),a)=Φ⁡(s,a,u⁡(m))\varphi((s,m),a)=\Phi(s,a,u(m)). Next, given κ\kappa i.i.d. samples ξ1,…,ξκ∼m\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{\kappa}\sim m, define the empirical embedding u^κ​(m)≔1κ​∑j=1κψ⁡(ξj)\widehat{u}_{\kappa}(m)\coloneqq\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{j=1}^{\kappa}\psi(\xi_{j}) and set φκ​((s,m),a)≔Φ⁡(s,a,u^κ​(m))\varphi_{\kappa}((s,m),a)\coloneqq\Phi(s,a,\widehat{u}_{\kappa}(m)). Then for any (x,a)(x,a) and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, we have that for a universal constant C1C_{1},

|φκ(x,a)−φ(x,a)∥2≤C1p+log⁡(1/δ)κ=C1d+|𝒜|+log⁡(1/δ)κ.|\varphi_{\kappa}(x,a)-\varphi(x,a)\|_{2}\leq C_{1}\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(1/\delta)}{\kappa}}=C_{1}\sqrt{\frac{d+|\mathcal{A}|+\log(1/\delta)}{\kappa}}. (36)
Proof.

Fix any (x,a)=((s,m),a)(x,a)=((s,m),a). Then, from Lemma C.11, we have

‖φκ​(x,a)−φ⁡(x,a)‖2=‖Φ⁡(s,a,u^κ​(m))−Φ⁡(s,a,u⁡(m))‖2≤‖u^κ​(m)−u⁡(m)‖2.\|\varphi_{\kappa}(x,a)-\varphi(x,a)\|_{2}=\|\Phi(s,a,\widehat{u}_{\kappa}(m))-\Phi(s,a,u(m))\|_{2}\leq\|\widehat{u}_{\kappa}(m)-u(m)\|_{2}.

Let Δ≔u^κ​(m)−u⁡(m)=1κ​∑j=1κ(ψ⁡(ξj)−𝔼⁡[ψ⁡(ξj)])\Delta\coloneqq\widehat{u}_{\kappa}(m)-u(m)=\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{j=1}^{\kappa}\big(\psi(\xi_{j})-\mathbb{E}[\psi(\xi_{j})]\big). For any fixed unit vector v∈𝕊p−1v\in\mathbb{S}^{p-1}, the scalar random variables Yj​(v)≔⟨v,ψ⁡(ξj)⟩Y_{j}(v)\coloneqq\langle v,\psi(\xi_{j})\rangle satisfy |Yj​(v)|≤‖v‖2​‖ψ⁡(ξj)‖2≤1|Y_{j}(v)|\leq\|v\|_{2}\|\psi(\xi_{j})\|_{2}\leq 1 almost surely. Hence, by Hoeffding’s inequality,

Pr[|⟨v,Δ⟩|≥t]=Pr[|1κ∑j=1κ(Yj(v)−𝔼[Yj(v)])|≥t]≤2exp(−κ​t22).\Pr\!\left[\big|\langle v,\Delta\rangle\big|\geq t\right]=\Pr\!\left[\left|\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{j=1}^{\kappa}(Y_{j}(v)-\mathbb{E}[Y_{j}(v)])\right|\geq t\right]\leq 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{\kappa t^{2}}{2}\right).

|⟨v,Δ⟩|\displaystyle|\langle v,\Delta\rangle| ≤|⟨v~,Δ⟩|+|⟨v−v~,Δ⟩|\displaystyle\leq|\langle\tilde{v},\Delta\rangle|+|\langle v-\tilde{v},\Delta\rangle|
≤supu∈𝒩|⟨u,Δ⟩|+‖v−v~‖2​‖Δ‖2\displaystyle\leq\sup_{u\in\mathcal{N}}|\langle u,\Delta\rangle|+\|v-\tilde{v}\|_{2}\|\Delta\|_{2}

‖Δ‖2≤2​t=2​2​(p​log⁡5+log⁡(2/δ))κ≤C1​p+log⁡(1/δ)κ\|\Delta\|_{2}\leq 2t=2\sqrt{\frac{2(\,p\log 5+\log(2/\delta)\,)}{\kappa}}\leq C_{1}\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(1/\delta)}{\kappa}}

proving the claim.∎

Consequently, in the continuous state-action setting, as κ→n\kappa\to n and M→∞M\to\infty, the value function of the estimated policy converges to the optimal value function, i.e., Vπκ,m​(s,g)→Vπ∗​(s,g)V^{\pi_{\kappa,m}}(s,g)\to V^{\pi^{*}}(s,g). Intuitively, as the subsampling parameter κ\kappa approaches the population size nn, the optimality gap diminishes following the concentration arguments in Theorem 4.3. As the number of samples MM increases, the linear function approximation error vanishes, which allows for the exact recovery of the spectral representations.
